Though familiar with the rationalist tradition of Maimonides, he increasingly aligned with the more traditionalist and mystical orientation associated with Nachmanides and became alarmed by the spread of radical Aristotelianism among Jewish intellectuals in Provence.

name: Mordecai ben Hillel
bio: Mordecai ben Hillel (c. 1250–1298), commonly known simply as the Mordecai, was a leading German Talmudist and halakhic authority of medieval Ashkenazic Judaism. Born in the Holy Roman Empire, he studied under major Tosafist scholars including Meir of Rothenburg and became one of the foremost transmitters of late Tosafist legal traditions. His comprehensive halakhic compilation on the Talmud synthesized rulings and customs from German and French rabbinic authorities and became an important source for later codifiers. He and much of his family were killed during the Rintfleisch massacres that devastated Jewish communities in Germany at the end of the thirteenth century.

name: Yom Tov of Seville
bio: Yom Tov ben Abraham Ishbili (c. 1250–1330), commonly known as the Ritva, was one of the foremost Talmudists and halakhic authorities of medieval Sephardic Judaism. Born in Seville in Christian Spain, he later became active in Barcelona and other centers of Catalonian Jewish scholarship. A disciple of Solomon ben Aderet and Aaron HaLevi, he combined rigorous Talmudic analysis with broad familiarity with earlier Sephardic and Ashkenazic traditions. His Talmudic novellae became among the most influential commentaries in the Sephardic rabbinic tradition and remain central to advanced Talmud study.

name: Asher ben Jehiel
bio: Asher ben Jehiel (c. 1250–1327), commonly known as the Rosh, was one of the foremost medieval rabbinic authorities of Ashkenazic and Sephardic Judaism. Born in the Holy Roman Empire, likely in Cologne, he studied under Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg and became a leading Talmudic scholar in Germany. Following the imprisonment of his teacher and increasing persecutions against Jews in the German lands, he fled to Christian Spain, where he became rabbi of Toledo and established a major yeshiva. His halakhic rulings and Talmudic commentaries profoundly influenced later Jewish law, particularly through their incorporation into the Arba'ah Turim and later the Shulchan Arukh.

name: Jacob ben Asher
bio: Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), commonly known as the בעל הטורים (Ba'al HaTurim), was one of the most influential medieval halakhic codifiers of Jewish law. Born in Cologne in the Holy Roman Empire, he was the son of the eminent rabbinic authority Asher ben Jehiel. Following the persecutions and instability affecting German Jewry, he migrated with his father to Toledo in Spain, where he became immersed in the Sephardic intellectual world while preserving Ashkenazic legal traditions. His monumental legal code, the 'Arba'ah Turim', systematized Jewish law into four sections and became one of the principal foundations for later halakhic works, including the Shulchan Arukh.

name: יעקב בן אשר (Ba'al HaTurim)
bio: Rabbi Jacob ben Asher (c. 1269–1343), known as the Ba'al HaTurim or simply the Tur, was a major halakhic authority and the author of the Arba'ah Turim, the foundational code of Jewish law that systematized halakha into four sections. His work served as the basis for Rabbi Yosef Karo’s Shulchan Aruch. He was the son of Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel (the Rosh).

name: Gersonides
bio: Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), commonly known as Gersonides or by the acronym Ralbag, was a medieval Jewish philosopher, biblical commentator, mathematician, astronomer, and physician from Provence. Born in Bagnols-sur-Cèze in southern France, he became one of the foremost Jewish Aristotelian thinkers after Maimonides. Deeply influenced by philosophy and the sciences of the Islamic and Christian worlds, he sought to harmonize reason, astronomy, and Jewish theology. His works on mathematics and astronomy gained recognition beyond Jewish circles, while his biblical commentaries became enduring classics of rationalist Jewish exegesis.

name: David Abudarham
bio: David Abudarham (c. 1300–c. 1360) was a Spanish rabbi, liturgist, and commentator best known for his comprehensive exposition of the Jewish prayer liturgy. Born in Seville during the late medieval flourishing of Sephardic Jewry, he was a disciple of Jacob ben Asher, author of the Arba'ah Turim. Abudarham sought to explain the structure, origins, and meanings of Jewish prayers and customs, integrating halakhic, grammatical, and mystical traditions into a single accessible framework. His writings became highly influential throughout the Sephardic and later Ashkenazic worlds.

name: ר' וידאל די טולוסה (Vidal of Tolosa, Maggid Mishneh)
bio: Rabbi Vidal of Tolosa (14th century), known as the Maggid Mishneh, was a Spanish Talmudist and one of the foremost commentators on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah. His commentary, Maggid Mishneh, was widely accepted and printed in nearly all standard editions of the Mishneh Torah, becoming one of the classic works for understanding Maimonides’ rulings. He lived in Aragon (likely in Barcelona or surrounding regions) during the period of the Rishonim.

name: Nissim of Gerona
bio: Nissim ben Reuben of Gerona (c. 1310–1376), commonly known as the Ran, was one of the foremost rabbinic authorities, Talmudists, philosophers, and communal leaders of medieval Sephardic Jewry. Born in Barcelona and later active in Gerona, he studied under leading Catalonian scholars and became a central figure in the transmission of Spanish rabbinic learning during a period of political instability and growing anti-Jewish pressure. Renowned for his Talmudic novellae, halakhic rulings, and philosophical sermons, he combined rigorous legal analysis with broader ethical and theological reflection. His teachings strongly influenced later Sephardic scholarship and Jewish legal tradition.

name: Hasdai Crescas
bio: Hasdai Crescas (c. 1340–1410/1411) was a Spanish Jewish philosopher, halakhist, communal leader, and one of the most important critics of Aristotelian philosophy in medieval Judaism. Born in Barcelona during the later flourishing of Sephardic intellectual life, he studied under Nissim ben Reuben and became a prominent rabbinic authority in the Crown of Aragon. Deeply affected by the anti-Jewish persecutions of 1391, including the murder of his son, Crescas devoted himself to strengthening Jewish faith and communal resilience. His philosophical masterpiece 'Or Adonai' challenged Aristotelian metaphysics and influenced later Jewish and European thought, including Spinoza.

name: Joseph Albo
bio: Joseph Albo (c. 1380–1444) was a Spanish Jewish philosopher, theologian, and rabbi best known for his systematic presentation of the principles of Judaism in the late medieval period. Born in the Crown of Aragon, likely in Monreal del Campo, he studied under Hasdai Crescas and became deeply influenced by anti-Aristotelian Jewish philosophy. Albo lived during a period of increasing pressure on Spanish Jewry, including forced disputations and mass conversions. His major philosophical work, 'Sefer Ha-Ikkarim', sought to define the essential principles of Jewish faith while defending Judaism against Christian polemics and internal philosophical disputes.

name: Israel Isserlein
bio: Israel Isserlein (1390–1460), also known as Maharai, was one of the foremost Ashkenazic halakhic authorities of the late medieval period. Born in Regensburg during an era of upheaval for Central European Jewry, he studied under leading German and Austrian rabbis and became renowned for his mastery of Talmudic law and communal practice. He later settled in Wiener Neustadt, where he headed a major yeshiva that attracted students from across the Holy Roman Empire. His responsa and legal rulings became highly influential in shaping later Ashkenazic custom and halakhic practice, particularly through their incorporation into the works of Moses Isserles.

name: Isaac Abravanel
bio: Isaac Abravanel (1437–1508), also known as Don Isaac Abravanel, was a Portuguese Jewish statesman, financier, biblical commentator, and philosopher who played a major role in both Jewish and Iberian political history during the late medieval period. Born in Lisbon into a distinguished Sephardic family descended from Iberian Jewish nobility, he served in the royal courts of Portugal, Castile, and Naples while simultaneously producing major works of biblical exegesis and Jewish philosophy. Following the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492, he became one of the leading voices of Sephardic exile and renewal in the Mediterranean world.

name: Abarbanel
bio: Don Isaac Abarbanel (1437–1508) was a Portuguese-Jewish statesman, philosopher, and biblical commentator. He served as royal treasurer in Portugal, advisor to Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and later settled in Italy. He was a fierce opponent of Maimonidean rationalism, emphasizing redemption and messianic hope in his works. His biblical commentaries are widely studied for their historical and philosophical insights.

name: יעקב פולאק (Rabbi Jacob Pollak)
bio: Rabbi Jacob Pollak (c. 1460–1541) was a pioneering Talmudist and rosh yeshivah, regarded as the founder of the Polish method of pilpul (analytical dialectical study). He was a central figure in establishing Poland as a major center of Jewish learning in the 16th century.

name: Jacob Berab
bio: Jacob Berab (1474–1546) was a leading Sephardic rabbi, Talmudist, and halakhic authority of the early Ottoman period who played a central role in the revival of Jewish scholarship in Safed after the expulsion from Spain. Born in the Kingdom of Castile shortly before the expulsion of Spanish Jewry, he fled with his family to North Africa and later studied in the Ottoman Empire. He became renowned for his Talmudic brilliance and communal leadership, serving as chief rabbi in several communities before settling in Safed. There he attempted to revive the ancient institution of semikhah (rabbinic ordination), a controversial initiative that sparked major halakhic debates throughout the Jewish world.

name: ר׳ עובדיה ספורנו
bio: ר׳ עובדיה בן יעקב ספורנו (c.1475–1550), known simply as the Sforno, was an Italian rabbi, biblical commentator, philosopher and physician. Born at Cesena into a Jewish banking family, he pursued medicine and philosophy in Rome and taught Hebrew to the Christian humanist Johannes Reuchlin in 1498–1500. He obtained a medical degree at Ferrara in 1501, returned to Rome and became a prominent member of its Jewish community with access to papal circles. After the Sack of Rome in 1527, he settled in Bologna, where he practised medicine, served as a rabbi, taught a select circle and probably helped revive Hebrew printing. His philosophical אור עמים, printed in Bologna in 1537, challenged propositions of scholastic and Aristotelian philosophy that he considered incompatible with revelation; a revised Latin version, Lumen gentium, appeared in 1548. His concise commentary on the Torah combines close reading, ethical interpretation, rational inquiry and occasional medical knowledge. Most of his biblical commentaries, including the Torah commentary edited by his brother ר׳ חננאל ספורנו, appeared only after his death. He died in Bologna in 1550; subsequent expulsions and destruction of the Jewish cemetery left his burial place unidentified.
title: הספורנו

name: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra
bio: David ben Solomon ibn Abi Zimra (c. 1479–1573), commonly known as the Radbaz, was one of the foremost halakhic authorities of the early modern Sephardic world. Born in Spain shortly before the expulsion of the Jews in 1492, he migrated with his family to North Africa and later settled in Egypt, where he became chief rabbi of Cairo and head of a major yeshiva. Renowned for his vast halakhic responsa, he addressed legal, communal, and theological questions arising across the Ottoman and Mediterranean Jewish worlds. In his later years he relocated to Safed in the Land of Israel, joining the flourishing center of rabbinic scholarship and mysticism there.

name: דוד בן שלמה אבן זמרא (Radvaz)
bio: Rabbi David ben Solomon ibn Zimra (1479–1573), known as the Radvaz, was a leading halakhic authority, kabbalist, and chief rabbi of Egypt. He wrote thousands of responsa, which became foundational sources for later halakhic rulings. He was also active in Safed during the golden age of Kabbalah alongside Rabbi Yosef Karo and Rabbi Moshe Cordovero.

name: מאיר קצנלנבוגן
bio: Rabbi Meir ben Isaac Katzenellenbogen (c. 1482–1565), also known as the Maharam of Padua, was one of the leading Ashkenazi rabbinic authorities of 16th-century Italy. Born in Katzenelnbogen, Germany, he studied under Rabbi Jacob Pollak in Prague before moving to Padua, where he married into the Minz rabbinic family. He later became Chief Rabbi of Padua and a major halachic authority consulted throughout Europe, including by Rabbi משה איסרליש (Rema). He is especially remembered for his responsa, his involvement in early Hebrew printing controversies, and his defense of Jewish publishing rights during the Bragadin-Giustiniani dispute.

name: יוסף קארו (Rabbi Yosef Karo)
bio: Rabbi Yosef Karo (1488–1575), known as the Mechaber, was the leading halakhic authority of his generation and author of the Shulchan Aruch, the most influential code of Jewish law. Born in Spain or Portugal, he was exiled as a child, lived in the Ottoman Empire, and eventually settled in Safed, where he became the head of the rabbinic court and a central figure in Jewish law and mysticism.

name: שלמה הלוי אלקבץ (Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz)
bio: Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi Alkabetz (c.1505–1584) was a Kabbalist, poet, and rabbinic leader of Safed. He is best known as the author of the mystical hymn Lecha Dodi, sung worldwide to welcome Shabbat. Teacher of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero and close associate of the Safed circle of mystics, he helped spread Kabbalat Shabbat and Zoharic practices.

name: שלמה לוריא (Maharshal)
bio: Rabbi Shlomo Luria (1510–1573), known as the Maharshal, was one of the greatest halakhists of Poland. He served as head of the yeshivah in Lublin, where many leading scholars studied under him. He authored Yam shel Shlomo, a major halakhic commentary on the Talmud, and Chokhmat Shlomo on the Shulchan Aruch.

name: שלום שכנא מלובלין (Rabbi Shalom Shachna of Lublin)
bio: Rabbi Shalom Shachna (c. 1510–1558) was a leading Polish rabbi and head of the first great yeshivah in Lublin, making the city the center of Jewish learning in Poland. A disciple of Rabbi Jacob Pollak, he was one of the earliest exponents of pilpul. He was also the teacher and father-in-law of Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema).

name: יהודה ליווא בן בצלאל (Maharal of Prague)
bio: Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel (ca. 1520–1609), known as the Maharal of Prague, was a leading rabbinic authority, philosopher, kabbalist, and communal leader. He is famous for his works on ethics, philosophy, and mysticism, and in legend, for creating the Golem of Prague.

name: בצלאל אשכנזי (Shita Mekubetzet)
bio: Rabbi Bezalel Ashkenazi (1520–1592) was a leading Egyptian rabbi and Talmudist, best known as the author of the Shita Mekubetzet, a monumental compendium of Talmudic commentaries. A disciple of Rabbi David ibn Abi Zimra (Radbaz) and teacher of the Arizal and Rabbi Chaim Vital, he played a central role in the transmission of Talmudic and Kabbalistic traditions.

name: משה קורדובירו (Ramak)
bio: Rabbi Moshe ben Yaakov Cordovero (1522–1570), known as the Ramak, was a preeminent Kabbalist in Safed before the Arizal. He synthesized and systematized earlier Kabbalistic teachings into a unified philosophy. His works profoundly influenced later Kabbalah, Hasidism, and Jewish thought.

name: הרב מרדכי יפה
bio: Rabbi Mordechai Yoffe (c.1530–1612), known as the Levush, was a major rabbinic authority and halakhist of Poland and Lithuania. A disciple of the Rema and Maharshal, he served as rabbi in Prague, Grodno, Lublin, and other communities. He is best remembered for his halakhic code 'Levushim' (Ten Garments), which systematized Jewish law after the Shulchan Aruch while incorporating Ashkenazic customs.

name: משה איסרליש (Rema)
bio: Rabbi Moshe Isserles (c. 1530–1572), known as the Rema, was the leading halakhic authority of Polish Jewry. His glosses on Rabbi Yosef Karo’s Shulchan Aruch, called HaMapah (the 'Tablecloth'), integrated Ashkenazic traditions into Karo’s Sephardic code, ensuring its universal acceptance. He was also a philosopher, Kabbalist, and communal leader in Kraków.

name: Arizal
bio: Rabbi Yitzchak Luria Ashkenazi (1534–1572), universally known as the Arizal or HaAri HaKadosh, was the central figure of Safed Kabbalah and the founder of Lurianic Kabbalah. Born in Jerusalem and raised largely in Egypt, he studied both revealed and mystical Torah before settling in Safed, where he transformed Jewish mysticism through profound teachings concerning creation, exile, redemption, reincarnation, and the spiritual structure of the universe. Although he wrote little himself, his disciple Rabbi Chaim Vital preserved and transmitted his teachings, which profoundly influenced later Kabbalah, Hasidism, Sephardic spirituality, and Jewish liturgy.

name: ר׳ חיים ויטאל
bio: ר׳ חיים ויטאל (1542–1620), known by the acronym מהרח״ו and also as Chaim Vital Calabrese, was the principal recorder and transmitter of the teachings of ר׳ יצחק לוריא, the האר״י. Born in Safed to the scribe Joseph Vital Calabrese, whose family originated in Calabria, he studied revealed Torah under ר׳ משה אלשיך and Kabbalah in the intellectual world shaped by ר׳ משה קורדובירו. When the האר״י settled in Safed in 1570, ר׳ חיים became his leading disciple and recorded the new Lurianic system during the master's final two years. After 1572 he organized a circle of disciples and asserted authority over the transmission of those teachings, although other disciples circulated competing recensions. His movements took him through Egypt, Ein al-Zeitun, Jerusalem, Safed and finally Damascus, where he taught Kabbalah and led a scholarly circle. His writings include his own ethical-mystical שערי קדושה, biblical commentary עץ הדעת טוב and autobiographical dream diary ספר החזיונות, alongside the enormous record of the האר״י's teachings later arranged by his son ר׳ שמואל ויטאל as שמונה שערים. Familiar titles such as עץ חיים and שער הגלגולים emerged through several manuscript recensions and later editors, so their attribution requires bibliographic caution. His record became the principal channel through which Lurianic Kabbalah transformed Sephardi spirituality, European Kabbalah, liturgy and later Hasidism.
title: מהרח״ו, תלמידו המובהק של האר״י ועורך קבלת האר״י

name: ר׳ שלמה אפרים מלונטשיץ
bio: ר׳ שלמה אפרים בן ר׳ אהרן מלונטשיץ (c. 1550–1619), known as the בעל כלי יקר, was one of the leading Polish-Jewish preachers, biblical commentators and communal rabbis of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Born in Łęczyca—rendered Luntschitz in Jewish sources—he was originally named אפרים; שלמה was added during a life-threatening illness, as he records in his introduction to כלי יקר. He studied under ר׳ שלמה לוריא (מהרש״ל) in Lublin and later headed a yeshiva in Lviv. His early publications established him as a moralist and master preacher: עיר גיבורים appeared in 1580, עוללות אפרים in 1590 and אורח לחיים in 1595. His best-known work, כלי יקר, was first printed in Lublin in 1602. It combines close biblical reading, midrash, moral psychology and public rebuke, frequently criticizing social inequality, ostentation, corrupt leadership and sterile methods of study. In 1604 he was appointed rabbi and prominent preacher in Prague, serving the community during the generation of ר׳ יהודה ליווא בן בצלאל (מהר״ל). His Prague writings included שפתי דעת and עמודי שש. He also composed penitential poems after violence struck Prague in 1611. His students and intellectual circle helped transmit Polish Torah learning into Bohemia; later tradition counts figures such as ר׳ יום טוב ליפמן הלר among those influenced by him. He died in Prague in 1619 and was buried in its Old Jewish Cemetery. כלי יקר remains widely printed in editions of the Torah and מקראות גדולות.
title: בעל כלי יקר
aliases: ר׳ שלמה אפרים בן אהרן לונטשיץ

name: שמואל אליעזר איידלס (Maharsha)
bio: Rabbi Shmuel Eidels (1555–1631), known as the Maharsha, was one of the greatest Talmudic commentators. His glosses on the Talmud, Chiddushei Halachot and Chiddushei Aggadot, are printed in virtually every edition of the Talmud. He served as rosh yeshivah in several Polish–Lithuanian communities, supported by his wealthy mother-in-law, Eidels, whose name he adopted.

name: ר' אברהם די בוטון (Abraham de Boton, Lechem Mishneh)
bio: Rabbi Abraham de Boton (c. 1560–c. 1605) was a leading Sephardic rabbi in the Ottoman Empire and the author of Lechem Mishneh, a foundational commentary on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah. He lived and taught in Salonika and later in Adrianople (Edirne), where he headed a prominent yeshiva. His Lechem Mishneh is printed in virtually all standard editions of the Mishneh Torah and remains a central commentary in halakhic study.

name: יואל סירקיש (Bach)
bio: Rabbi Joel ben Samuel Sirkis (1561–1640), known as the Bach after his halakhic work Bayit Chadash, was a leading Polish rabbi and posek. He served as rabbi of several major communities including Belz, Brest-Litovsk, and Kraków. His Bayit Chadash critically analyzed the Tur, correcting errors and integrating halakhic rulings. He was also the father-in-law of the Taz.

name: R' Yoshiyahu Pinto
bio: R' Yoshiyahu Pinto(c. 1565 – c. 1648) was a Syrian rabbi and preacher born in Damascus. His father, Joseph Pinto, was one of the wealthy and charitable men of that city. He studied Talmud and Kabbalah under various rabbis, and later, after his father's death, he studied under Jacob Abulafia, who ordained him as rabbi. Pinto lived primarily in Damascus, serving as rabbi until his death in Feb.–Mar. 1648. He briefly moved to Aleppo and to Safed in 1625, but returned to Damascus after the death of his young son Joseph.

name: דוד הלוי סגל (Taz – Turei Zahav)
bio: Rabbi David HaLevi Segal (c. 1586–1667), known as the Taz, was one of the foremost halakhic authorities in Poland. His commentary on the Shulchan Aruch, Turei Zahav (טורי זהב), became a standard part of halakhic literature, often printed together with the Shulchan Aruch. He studied under Rabbi Shlomo Ephraim Luntschitz (Keli Yakar) and was son-in-law of Rabbi Joel Sirkis (the Bach).

name: שבתי בן מאיר הכהן (Shabbatai ben Meir HaKohen, the Shakh)
bio: Talmudist and halakhist (1621–1662), known as the Shakh for his Siftei Kohen commentary on the Shulchan Aruch. Born in Lithuania, he became a leading authority of Jewish law in Poland and Moravia. His works, especially on Choshen Mishpat, were accepted as decisive halachic rulings.

name: ר׳ שבתי משורר בס
bio: ר׳ שבתי בן ר׳ יוסף משורר בס (1641–1718), best known as the author of שפתי חכמים, was a biblical commentator, cantor, bibliographer and pioneering Hebrew printer. Born in Kalisz, he lost his parents in the persecutions of 1655 and fled to Prague. There he studied Talmud under ר׳ מאיר וֶרטֶרס, learned music from ר׳ לייב שיר השירים and sang bass in Prague’s Altneuschul; his vocal part produced the names Bass, Bassista and משורר. From 1674 to 1679 he visited Jewish scholarly centres and libraries across Poland, Germany and Holland. In Amsterdam he learned printing and proofreading and in 1680 issued שפתי חכמים, a concise guide to difficulties in רש״י’s Torah commentary, alongside שפתי ישנים, the first substantial bibliography of Hebrew books. After securing official permission, he established a Hebrew press at Dyhernfurth in 1689. The enterprise attracted Jewish workers and helped create a durable local community; his descendants continued it. A fire damaged the press in 1708. In 1712 Jesuit accusations led to his arrest and the confiscation of books, though he was ultimately acquitted. He later returned to Poland and died in Krotoszyn. His commentary remained widely printed beside רש״י, while שפתי ישנים made him a founder of Hebrew bibliography.
title: בעל שפתי חכמים

name: Rabbi David Nieto
bio: Rabbi David Nieto (1654–1728) was the Haham of the Spanish and Portuguese Jewish community of London. A polymath, he wrote works on astronomy, medicine, and theology, defending traditional Judaism against deist and Karaite challenges.

name: Chacham Tzvi (Rabbi Zvi Ashkenazi)
bio: Rabbi Zvi Ashkenazi (1656–1718), known as the Chacham Tzvi, was a renowned Talmudist and halakhic authority. He served as Chief Rabbi of Amsterdam and opposed the spread of Sabbateanism.

name: Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart
bio: Rabbi Aaron Uri Phoebus Hart (1670–1756) was a British rabbi, widely regarded as the first chief rabbi of Great Britain. Born in Breslau, Silesia, to Hartwig Moses Hart, he studied in Poland and married the daughter of R. Samuel ben Phoebus of Fürth. In 1704/5 he was appointed rabbi of the first Ashkenazic synagogue in London, the Great Synagogue at Duke’s Place, where he served until his death. His tenure was marked by communal disputes, most notably the controversy surrounding Marcus Moses and the Hambro synagogue. In 1707 he published 'Urim ve-Tummim,' the first Hebrew book printed entirely in London. A portrait of Rabbi Hart is preserved in the National Portrait Gallery, London.

name: Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka
bio: Rabbi Nachman of Horodenka (c. 1680 – 1765) was among the earliest figures of the Hasidic movement and one of the closest disciples of the Baal Shem Tov, who referred to him as 'the trustee of his house.' He was known for his righteousness, his dedication to the redemption of captives, and his ascetic way of life even before Hasidism was founded. Through his descendants he became the grandfather of Rabbi Nachman of Breslov. Rabbi Nachman immigrated to the Land of Israel and settled in Tiberias, where his presence greatly impressed contemporaries. He passed away in Tiberias on 2 Tammuz 5525 (1765) and was buried in the Baal Shem Tov Students' Plot in the ancient cemetery of Tiberias.

name: Rabbi Joseph ben Emanuel Ergas
bio: Rabbi Joseph ben Emanuel Ergas (1685–1730) was an Italian rabbi and kabbalist, renowned for his erudition and as a fierce critic of Sabbateanism. Born in Livorno to Rabbi Emanuel Ergas, head of the community, he studied Torah under Rabbi Samuel De Pas and briefly Kabbalah under Rabbi Benjamin Kohen Vitale, a disciple of Moses Zacuto. After marrying in 1704, he founded the 'Noah Shalom' yeshiva in Pisa, and established charities such as Mohar Batulot and Malbish Aryamin. Returning to Livorno, he became head of the community and a leading halakhic authority, answering questions from rabbis throughout Italy and France. His most famous disciple was Rabbi Malachi ben Jacob ha-Kohen, author of Yad Malachi. Ergas became especially noted for his polemics against the Sabbatean Neḥemiah Ḥayyun, whom he expelled from Livorno in 1710, and against Sabbatean ideology in general. He authored works including the anti-Sabbatean tracts Tokhaḥat Meguleh and Ha-Tzad Naḥash, and the kabbalistic classic Shomer Emunim, which defended the non-literal interpretation of tzimtzum. He died in Livorno in 1730 at age 45.

name: ר׳ נתנאל וייל
bio: ר׳ נתנאל בן ר׳ נפתלי צבי וייל (1687–1769), remembered as the בעל קרבן נתנאל, was a leading German-Bohemian Talmudist, rosh yeshiva and regional rabbi. Born in Stühlingen into a learned family descended from ר׳ יעקב וייל (מהרי״ו), he was orphaned young: his father and a brother were murdered in 1692. At ten he was taken to Fürth and then sent to Prague, where his uncle ר׳ ליפמן וייל raised him. He studied under ר׳ אברהם ברודא, who later arranged his marriage to a niece, פייגלא, in 1708. ר׳ נתנאל accompanied his teacher westward before returning to Prague in 1717. There he served as an assistant rabbi and prominent yeshiva teacher, reportedly educating a very large body of students. Maria Theresa’s expulsion of Prague’s Jews in 1744 forced another migration. In 1745 he became regional rabbi of the Black Forest communities, based at Mühringen, and in 1750 was appointed chief regional rabbi of the Baden-Baden and Baden-Durlach territories at Karlsruhe. He completed קרבן נתנאל there and published it in 1755—the first Hebrew book printed in Karlsruhe. Its precise textual and halakhic commentary on the rulings of ר׳ אשר בן יחיאל for the Talmudic orders מועד and נשים became standard in editions of the Talmud. He died during a visit to Rastatt and was buried in Karlsruhe. His son ר׳ ידידיה טיאה וייל succeeded him and helped preserve his writings.
title: בעל קרבן נתנאל
aliases: ר׳ נתנאל בן נפתלי צבי וייל

name: Rabbi Jonathan Eybeschutz
bio: Rabbi Jonathan Eybeschutz (1690–1764) was a prominent rabbi, preacher, and Talmudist, serving as Rabbi of Metz and later as Chief Rabbi of the Three Communities (Altona, Hamburg, Wandsbek). Famous for his erudition, he was embroiled in the Emden-Eybeschutz controversy.

name: ר׳ חיים בן עטר (אור החיים הקדוש)
bio: ר׳ חיים בן משה בן עטר (1696–1743), universally known from his Torah commentary as the אור החיים הקדוש, was a Moroccan Sephardi Torah commentator, halakhist, Talmudist, preacher and kabbalist. Born in Salé, he learned first from his grandfather and namesake ר׳ חיים בן עטר הזקן. Political insecurity took the family to Meknes during his childhood, after which he taught in Salé and later Fez. Economic pressure, famine and his aspiration to establish a major academy in the Land of Israel shaped his departure from Morocco. After passing through Algiers, he built a circle of patrons and students in Livorno, arranged publication of his writings in Amsterdam and Venice, and sailed with his wives and roughly thirty disciples to Acre in 1741. Epidemics delayed entry into Jerusalem, so the group spent about a year in the Galilee before settling there in 1742. In Jerusalem he founded מדרש כנסת ישראל, with divisions for advanced revealed Torah and kabbalistic study; ר׳ חיים יוסף דוד אזולאי was among the scholars associated with his academy. He died after less than a year in Jerusalem and was buried on the Mount of Olives. His אור החיים combines close textual interpretation, halakhic reasoning, homily and kabbalistic theology and became especially influential across Sephardi, North African and Hasidic communities. Miraculous stories and an intended meeting with ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב belong to later devotional tradition and are not treated here as independently documented travel.
title: אור החיים הקדוש

name: Rabbi Jacob Emden
bio: Rabbi Jacob Emden (1697–1776) was a German rabbi, scholar, and fierce opponent of Sabbateanism. A prolific writer, he is remembered for his halakhic responsa, polemics, and for his heated disputes with Rabbi Jonathan Eybeschutz.

name: ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב
bio: ר׳ ישראל בן אליעזר בעל שם טוב (traditionally 1698–1760), known as the Baal Shem Tov or Besht, was a healer, religious mystic and charismatic leader in Polish Podolia, regarded as the founder of modern Hasidism. Tradition locates his birth at Okopy, but nearly all accounts of his childhood and early adulthood come from later Hasidic hagiography; contemporary evidence becomes substantial only during his mature career. He worked in Podolian towns, reportedly as a teacher, ritual slaughterer and circumciser, learned rabbinic literature and practical and contemplative Kabbalah, and became known during the 1730s as a baal shem—one who healed and mediated spiritual or personal difficulties. His wife Chana was the sister of ר׳ אברהם גרשון מקיטוב; their children were Tzvi Hirsh and Udl, whose descendants became important Hasidic leaders. In 1740 he settled at Medzhybizh, where estate records document a tax-exempt communal house and identify its occupant successively as a kabbalist, baal shem and “baal shem doctor.” He led a circle of scholarly mystics that included ר׳ יעקב יוסף מפולנאה, ר׳ דב בער ממזריטש, ר׳ פנחס מקוריץ and ר׳ נחמן מהורודנקה. His teachings emphasized divine presence throughout existence, prayer with attachment and intention, joy, humility and service through ordinary material life. He authored no systematic book. His sayings survive chiefly through students’ writings, later anthologies and a small, textually disputed body of letters. He died and was buried in Medzhybizh in 1760; his disciples transformed his circle into a durable movement after his death.

title: הבעל שם טוב — מייסד החסידות

name: Haham Isaac Nieto
bio: Isaac Nieto (1702–1774) was Haham of the Portuguese congregation Sha'are Hashamayim (Bevis Marks), London, and the son of David Nieto. He was officially appointed as Haham in 1733 but resigned in 1741 and travelled abroad. Returning in 1747, he became a notary and later, in 1749, established the Shaar Hashamayim congregation in Gibraltar, becoming its first rabbi. In 1751 he returned to London to serve as Av Bet Din, but resigned in 1757 after disputes. Nieto also preached a notable sermon in 1756 and published important Spanish-English translations of the prayer book. He died in London in 1774.

name: ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש
bio: ר׳ דוב בער בן אברהם (c.1704–15 December 1772), the Maggid of Mezeritch, was the principal organizer and systematic teacher of the second generation of Hasidism. Born at Lokachi in Volhynia, he received advanced rabbinic education traditionally associated with ר׳ יעקב יהושע פאלק, author of פני יהושע. Before entering the Hasidic circle he lived as an ascetic kabbalist and served as a preacher in Volhynian communities including Turchyn, Korets and Rivne. In the mid-eighteenth century he became a disciple of ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב at Medzhybizh; the encounter redirected his spirituality from bodily mortification toward divine immanence, joy and devekut. After the Baal Shem Tov's death in 1760, most of the emerging movement's leadership gathered around the Maggid at Mezhirichi. His relatively stationary court trained and dispatched a network of disciples—including ר׳ מנחם מנדל מוויטבסק, ר׳ שניאור זלמן מלאדי, ר׳ לוי יצחק מברדיטשוב, ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק and ר׳ אהרן הגדול מקרלין—who spread Hasidism across Eastern Europe. The Maggid wrote no systematic book; students edited oral teachings into מגיד דבריו ליעקב and related collections. He moved to Hannopil during a 1772 epidemic, died there on 19 Kislev 5533 and was buried in its Jewish cemetery.

title: המגיד ממזריטש — המגיד הגדול

name: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto (Ramchal)
bio: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto (1707–1746), known by the acronym Ramchal, was an Italian rabbi, kabbalist, philosopher, and poet. Born in Padua, he displayed extraordinary literary and mystical gifts from a young age. At 20 he claimed to receive teachings from a maggid (angelic guide), which brought him into sharp controversy with leading rabbis who feared a recurrence of the Sabbatean crisis. Forced to cease mystical writing, he left Italy for Amsterdam in 1735, where he worked as a diamond cutter and wrote his greatest works: Mesillat Yesharim, Derech Hashem, Da’at Tevunot, and Derech Tevunot. In 1743 he immigrated to the Land of Israel and settled in Acre, where he and his family died in a plague in 1746. His works became cornerstones of Jewish thought, particularly embraced by the Mussar movement a century later. He is remembered both as a foundational kabbalist and as the father of modern Hebrew literature.

name: Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk (Baal Shem of London)
bio: Rabbi Hayyim Samuel Jacob Falk (1708–1782), known as the Baal Shem of London and Doctor Falckon, was a rabbi, kabbalist, alchemist, and wonder-worker. Born in either Fürth (Bavaria) or Pidhaytsi (Podolia), he narrowly escaped execution in Westphalia on charges of sorcery and was sheltered by Count Alexander von Rantzau in Holzminden, where his mystical feats were witnessed by noblemen in 1736. Later he settled in London, living in Prescott Street and Wellclose Square, and was said to have influenced Emanuel Swedenborg. Accused by some, including Rabbi Jacob Emden, of Sabbatean associations, he nonetheless became a legendary figure in Jewish folklore. He died on 17 April 1782 and was buried in Alderney Road Cemetery, London. Falk left a bequest of £100 annually to the Great Synagogue of London and several Torah scrolls. His diary, recording kabbalistic dreams and angelic names, survives in the United Synagogue library.

name: שמואל מרגליות (Shmuel Margolies)
bio: Rabbi Shmuel ben Uri Shraga Feivish Margolies (1711–1790), known as the Maharam Margolies, was a prominent rabbi in Galicia and later one of the first great rabbinic authorities in the American colonies. He immigrated to New York in 1730s and served as rabbi of Congregation Shearith Israel, the Spanish-Portuguese synagogue, making him one of the earliest recognized rabbis in North America.

name: ר׳ יחזקאל הלוי לנדא
bio: ר׳ יחזקאל בן ר׳ יהודה הלוי לנדא (7 November 1713–29 April 1793), known as the נודע ביהודה and הצל״ח, was an eighteenth-century halakhic authority, communal rabbi and head of the Prague yeshivah. Born at Opatów, he entered the renowned Brody kloyz after his marriage and became a dayan there. In 1745 he became rabbi and head of the academy at Yampol. His 1752 אגרת השלום attempted to mediate the dispute between ר׳ יעקב עמדין and ר׳ יהונתן אייבשיץ. Appointed chief rabbi of Prague in 1754/1755, he led the community for nearly four decades through Habsburg reforms, war and Jewish religious controversies. His responsa נודע ביהודה address practical questions from across Europe; its first edition appeared at Prague in 1776 and a second, posthumous series in 1810/1811. His other writings include דגול מרבבה and ציון לנפש חיה. He died in Prague on 17 Iyar 5553 and was buried in the Žižkov Jewish cemetery.
title: הנודע ביהודה — הצל״ח

name: ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק
bio: ר׳ אלימלך בן ר׳ אליעזר ליפמן (1717–11 March 1787), known as ר׳ אלימלך מליז׳נסק and by the title of his book נועם אלימלך, was an early Hasidic leader who established Hasidism as a durable movement in Galicia and Poland. He was born at Łopuchowo near Tykocin in Podlasie, into a prosperous rural family. In his earlier religious life he practiced severe asceticism and undertook a voluntary wandering exile with his brother ר׳ משולם זושא מאניפולי. Through his brother he entered the Hasidic circle and became a leading disciple of ר׳ דוב בער ממזריטש. After the Maggid's death in 1772, ר׳ אלימלך settled at Leżajsk, which became the principal center from which he trained leaders including ר׳ יעקב יצחק הורוביץ מלובלין, ר׳ ישראל הופשטיין מקוז׳ניץ, ר׳ מנחם מנדל מרימנוב and ר׳ אברהם יהושע השל מאפטא. His teachings developed the social and spiritual role of the tsaddik as guide and intercessor. His son ר׳ אלעזר and other family members and editors preserved his Sabbath discourses and published נועם אלימלך posthumously at Lemberg in 1788. He died at Leżajsk on 21 Adar 5547 and was buried there.

title: הנועם אלימלך — הרבי ר׳ אלימלך

name: Rabbi Eliyahu ben Shlomo Zalman (Vilna Gaon, Gra)
bio: Rabbi Eliyahu ben Shlomo Zalman (1720–1797), known as the Vilna Gaon or simply 'the Gra', was the preeminent Lithuanian Talmudist, halakhist, kabbalist, and leader of the Misnagdic (non-Hasidic) world. Born in Sialiec near Brisk, he showed prodigious genius from childhood, mastering Tanakh, Talmud, and Kabbalah by age ten. He lived most of his life in Vilna, where he devoted himself entirely to Torah study, refusing formal rabbinic office but guiding Lithuanian Jewry through his writings and students. His glosses and emendations to the Talmud, Shulchan Aruch, Tanakh, and kabbalistic works revolutionized Jewish study. The Vilna Gaon fiercely opposed the Hasidic movement, signing bans of excommunication in 1772 and 1781, and his disciples founded the great Lithuanian yeshiva tradition, beginning with Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin. He also valued mathematics, astronomy, and other sciences as aids to Torah but condemned secular philosophy. He passed away in Vilna on 9 October 1797 (19 Tishrei 5558). His influence continues through the 'minhag ha-Gra' and his central place in the Litvak tradition.

name: Rabbi Sar Shalom Mizraḥi Sharabi (Rashash)
bio: Rabbi Sar Shalom Mizraḥi Sharabi (1720–1777), known as the Rashash, was a Yemenite rabbi, halachist, chazzan, and kabbalist. Born in Sharab, Yemen, he left for Jerusalem in fulfillment of a vow, passing through India, Baghdad, and Damascus. In Damascus, he engaged in halachic debate regarding the measure of a kezayit of matzah. In Jerusalem, he joined the circle of mekubalim at the Beit El Yeshiva, where his extraordinary piety and hidden mastery of Lurianic Kabbalah were gradually revealed. He rose to become Rosh Yeshiva of Beit El, leading the foremost kabbalistic academy of the time. He was deeply devoted to the teachings of Rabbi Isaac Luria and developed new methods of kavanot (mystical prayer meditations). Popular tradition recounts miracles associated with him, including resisting seduction in Yemen, an appearance of the prophet Elijah, and opening access for Jews to the Kotel. He was regarded by many as the gilgul (reincarnation) of the Arizal. His descendants included Chief Rabbi Chaim Abraham Gagin and later Shem Tob Gaguine. The Rashash passed away in Jerusalem in 1777 and was buried on the Mount of Olives. His yahrzeit is still commemorated annually by kabbalists and members of Beit El.

name: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch (Hirschel) Levin (Berlin)
bio: Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Levin (1721–1800), also known as Zvi Hirsch Berlin, Hart Lyon, and Hirsch Levin, was one of the leading Ashkenazi rabbis of the 18th century. Born in Rzeszów to Rabbi Aryeh Leib (later Rabbi of Amsterdam) and Miriam, daughter of the Chacham Tzvi, he was the nephew of Rabbi Yaakov Emden. Alongside his Talmudic education, he studied philosophy, natural sciences, and Hebrew grammar. In 1751 he sided with his uncle in the great dispute against Rabbi Yonatan Eybeschutz. In 1756 he became rabbi of the Great Synagogue of London, but resigned due to lax observance among congregants. He later served in Halberstadt and Mannheim before being appointed Chief Rabbi of Berlin in 1772, at the dawn of the Haskalah. Unlike many Polish rabbis, Levin took a moderate stance: opposing Enlightenment excesses but accepting secular studies when subordinate to Torah. He maintained cordial relations with Moses Mendelssohn, giving approbation to Mendelssohn’s Pentateuch translation (1778), and commissioned Mendelssohn to compose 'Ritualgesetze der Juden' at government request. He faced fierce controversy over Naftali Hertz Wessely’s reforms (1782), pressured by traditional rabbis on one side and Berlin Maskilim on the other, briefly resigning before returning to his post until his death. His sons included Rabbi Shaul Berlin, embroiled in literary controversies, Rabbi Avraham David Tevil of Berlin, and Rabbi Shlomo Hirschel, the first Chief Rabbi of Britain.

name: Haim Yosef David Azulai (Hida)
bio: Rabbi Haim Yosef David Azulai (1724–1806), known by the acronym Hida, was a Jerusalem-born Sephardic rabbi, halakhist, kabbalist, bibliophile, and prolific author. A descendant of Rabbi Abraham Azulai, he studied under leading sages of Jerusalem including Rabbi Haim ibn Attar (Ohr HaHaim), Rabbi Shalom Sharabi, and Rabbi Yonah Nabon. Gifted with an extraordinary memory, he mastered Talmud, halakha, kabbalah, and Jewish history at a young age. Chosen as an emissary (shadar) for the Hebron community, he traveled extensively across Europe and North Africa (1753–1757; 1772–1778), strengthening ties with Diaspora communities and collecting funds for the Holy Land. His travel diaries, Ma’agal Tov, record Jewish life and his encounters with manuscripts, libraries, and rabbis across Europe. He authored over 70 works including halakhic commentaries such as Birkei Yosef, homiletics, liturgy, kabbalistic texts, and the seminal bibliographic-historical dictionary Shem HaGedolim, which preserves invaluable information on Jewish authors and texts. After his second marriage in Pisa in 1778, he settled in Livorno, a center of Jewish publishing, where he lived until his death in 1806. In 1960, his remains were reinterred in Jerusalem on Har HaMenuchot, fulfilling his wish to return to the Land of Israel.

name: Rabbi David ben Hassin
bio: Rabbi David ben Hassin (1727–1792) was one of the greatest Jewish poets of Morocco, whose piyyutim spread across the Maghreb and the Middle East. Born in the Mellah of Meknes, he studied under Rabbi Mordechai Birdugo and married his daughter. At 17, he authored his first work, Migdal LaDavid, on biblical exegesis and Torah study. He became a prolific poet, composing over 250 poems blending biblical, rabbinic, and liturgical Hebrew. His works, filled with themes of exile, suffering, consolation, and redemption, gave voice to Moroccan Jewry during a time of drought, persecution, and the brutal reign of Moulay Yazid. His poetry, including piyyutim such as 'Asdar Toshbechta,' was sung throughout Moroccan communities and later adopted in Yemen and other Eastern Jewish traditions. After his death, many of his poems were compiled and published in Amsterdam in 1867 as 'Tehillah LeDavid' (Praise for David), ensuring his legacy as a central poet of Sephardic Jewry.

name: Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz (Ba'al Hafla'ah)
bio: Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz (1730–1805), known as the 'Ba'al Hafla’ah,' was the Rabbi of Frankfurt and a leading halakhist, disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, and a bridge between Hasidic and Misnagdic worlds.

name: Rabbi Raphael Hayyim Isaac Carregal
bio: Rabbi Raphael Hayyim Isaac Carregal (1733–1777) was an itinerant rabbi and preacher from Hebron, regarded as the first rabbi known to have visited the American colonies. Ordained at 17, he spent his life traveling widely, serving in Constantinople, Curaçao, London, Jamaica, North America, Suriname, and Barbados. In 1773, while in Newport, Rhode Island, he befriended Ezra Stiles, future president of Yale, with whom he studied Hebrew, discussed biblical exegesis, and corresponded extensively in Hebrew. Carregal’s sermons, published in Newport in 1773, are the first known Jewish sermons printed in the United States. He died in Barbados in 1777 at the age of 43.

name: Rabbi Aharon Perlov of Karlin (the Great)
bio: Rabbi Aharon Perlov of Karlin (1736–1772), known as Rabbi Aharon the Great, was one of the earliest Rebbes of the Hasidic movement and a disciple of Rabbi Dov Ber of Mezeritch, the Maggid. He founded the Karlin Hasidic dynasty in Karlin, near Pinsk, and together with Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk spread Hasidism throughout Lithuania. Opponents of the Hasidic movement often referred to all Hasidim as 'Karlins' due to his influence. He was known for introducing fervent, emotional prayer marked by great enthusiasm and shouting, a hallmark of Karlin Hasidism to this day. He authored the famous piyyut 'Ya Aksuf', sung in many Hasidic courts on Shabbat. He passed away at the young age of 36, leaving behind a legacy of passionate devotion and outreach. His disciple Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin succeeded him, raising his son Rabbi Asher of Stolin, continuing the Karlin-Stolin dynasty.

name: Rabbi Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev (Kedushas Levi)
bio: Rabbi Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev (1740–1809), also known as the Kedushas Levi and the 'Holy Berdichever,' was one of the most beloved Hasidic masters and leaders of Eastern European Jewry. A close disciple of the Maggid of Mezritch and Rabbi Shmelke of Nikolsburg, he served as rabbi in Ryczywół, Żelechów, Pinsk, and most famously Berdichev, where he became known as the 'defense attorney of the Jewish people' for his compassionate prayers and advocacy on behalf of all Jews before God. Nachman of Breslov called him the 'Glory of Israel.' He was known for fiery devotion, boundless love for every Jew, and authored the Hasidic classic 'Kedushas Levi,' a Torah commentary blending Halakhah, Midrash, and Hasidic philosophy. His songs, including 'A Dude'le' and 'A Din Toyre mit Gott,' remain part of Jewish folk and spiritual heritage.

name: Alter of Liadi
bio: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi (1745–1812), known as the 'Alter Rebbe,' was the founder of Chabad Hasidism and author of the Tanya and Shulchan Aruch HaRav. He was a leading disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch.

name: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Kahana Heller (Ketzos HaChoshen)
bio: Rabbi Aryeh Leib ben Yosef Kahana Heller (c. 1745–1812) was a Galician rabbi, Talmudist, and halachist, best known for his magnum opus 'Ketzos HaChoshen.' Born in Kalush, he was a fifth-generation descendant of Rabbi Yom-Tov Lipmann Heller and the youngest of five brothers, including Rabbi Yehuda Heller, author of 'Kuntras HaSfeikos.' He studied under Rabbi Meshulam Igra of Tysmienica, becoming recognized as one of the foremost halachic authorities of his era. From 1788 until his death in 1812, he served as rabbi of Stryi, where he often engaged in halachic debates with his contemporary Rabbi Yaakov Lorberbaum, author of 'Netivot ha-Mishpat.' A staunch misnaged and critic of Hasidism, his works became classics studied in all yeshivas, laying the groundwork for analytical Talmudic methodology.

name: Rabbi Raphael Berdugo (Archangel Raphael)
bio: Rabbi Raphael Berdugo (1747–1821), known as the 'Archangel Raphael,' was one of Morocco’s greatest rabbis, halachic authorities, and communal leaders. Born into the distinguished Berdugo rabbinic dynasty of Meknes, he was the grandson of Rabbi Moshe Berdugo ('Hamashbir') and son of Rabbi Mordechai Berdugo ('Marbitz'). Orphaned at fifteen, his brilliance in Torah was already recognized at his father’s memorial. Despite early poverty, he rose to become head of the Beit Din of Meknes and a leading posek of his generation. He enacted community regulations limiting ostentation, provided leadership during pogroms, droughts, and epidemics, and earned the reverent title 'Archangel Raphael.' His responsa and commentaries became foundational texts for Moroccan Jewry. He died on Hoshana Rabbah in 1821, at age 75, and his rulings continued to be revered long after his passing.

name: ר׳ אברהם דנציג
bio: ר׳ אברהם בן ר׳ יחיאל מיכל דנציג (1748–1820), universally known as בעל חיי אדם, was a merchant, Vilna dayan and one of the most influential modern codifiers of practical halakhah. Born in Danzig, he entered the Prague yeshiva at fourteen and studied with ר׳ יחזקאל לנדא and ר׳ יוסף ליברמן. He subsequently settled in Vilna but initially refused salaried rabbinic office, supporting his family through commerce and travelling to the fairs of Leipzig and Königsberg. His experience as both a major scholar and working householder shaped an unusually accessible legal project. חיי אדם reorganized the laws of אורח חיים around the rhythms of daily, Sabbath and festival life, while נשמת אדם supplied deeper legal analysis. חכמת אדם and בינת אדם performed a comparable service principally for יורה דעה. He critically sifted centuries of post–שולחן ערוך rulings rather than merely abridging them, and later authorities—including משנה ברורה—frequently cite his conclusions. A devastating Vilna gunpowder-magazine explosion in 1803 destroyed his home, injured his family and contributed to the loss of his fortune. He instituted the family’s annual פולווער־פורים thanksgiving and later accepted service as a dayan. His writing joined exacting halakhah to ethical instruction, lay education and practical religious discipline. תפילה זכה, printed in חיי אדם, became widely recited before Kol Nidrei. He hoped to settle in Jerusalem and wrote שערי צדק for laws dependent on the Land of Israel, but died in Vilna before realizing that plan.
title: בעל חיי אדם
aliases: ר׳ אברהם בן יחיאל מיכל דנציג

name: ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין
bio: ר׳ חיים איצקוביץ מוולוז׳ין (24 May 1749–14 June 1821), usually called ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין or Reb Chaim Volozhiner, was the leading disciple of ר׳ אליהו בן שלמה זלמן, the Vilna Gaon, and the institutional architect of the Lithuanian yeshivah tradition. Born in Volozhin to community leader ר׳ יצחק בן חיים and Rivka, he studied with ר׳ רפאל זיסקינד הכהן and ר׳ אריה לייב גינצבורג, author of שאגת אריה, before joining the Vilna Gaon’s circle. He served as rabbi of Volozhin, briefly held the rabbinate of Vilkomir/Ukmergė, and returned to his native town. In 1802 he circulated a public appeal for support; around 1803 he founded Yeshivat Etz Chaim, the Volozhin Yeshiva. Unlike the older local study-house model, it recruited advanced students from many communities, provided material support and organized continuous Torah study. It became the prototype for the great Lithuanian yeshivot. His posthumously published נפש החיים presents a kabbalistically informed theology of divine presence, prayer, mitzvot and especially Torah study; it engages ideas associated with Hasidism while articulating a distinct mitnagdic program. His son ר׳ יצחק מוולוז׳ין succeeded him and published נפש החיים. His teachings and institution shaped students including ר׳ זונדל מסלנט and enduring scholarly lineages associated with Volozhin, Brisk and the Musar movement.
title: ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין; בעל נפש החיים; מייסד ישיבת עץ חיים

name: Rav
bio: Rav Abba bar Aybo (175–247 CE), commonly known as Abba Arikha or simply as Rav, was one of the earliest and most influential Babylonian Amoraim. Born in Kafri in Babylonia, he studied in the Land of Israel under his uncle Rabbi Hiyya and was associated with the academy of Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi at Sepphoris. He returned to Babylonia in 219 CE, first teaching at Nehardea before establishing his own academy at Sura. Rav's school became a major centre of Jewish learning, and his teachings and debates, particularly those with Shmuel of Nehardea, form an important part of the Babylonian Talmud.

name: ר׳ נחמן מברסלב
bio: ר׳ נחמן בן שמחה ופייגא (1772–1810), known as ר׳ נחמן מברסלב, founded the Breslov school of Hasidism. Born in Medzhybizh, he was a maternal great-grandson of ר׳ ישראל בעל שם טוב and a paternal grandson of ר׳ נחמן מהורודנקה. After marrying young, he lived near his wife's family and then in Medvedivka, where he began attracting disciples. His dangerous 1798–1799 pilgrimage through Istanbul to Haifa, Tiberias and Safed—followed by escape from Acre during Napoleon's campaign—became a decisive spiritual turning point in his own account. After brief residence in Zlatopol, he settled in Bratslav in 1802; there ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ became his principal disciple, recorder and editor. ר׳ נחמן taught an intensely personal path centered on faith, joy amid spiritual struggle, daily hitbodedut or direct solitary speech with God, the role of the tzaddik, melody, storytelling and continual renewal. His claims and critique of contemporary Hasidic leadership provoked opposition, notably from ר׳ אריה לייב משפולה, while ר׳ לוי יצחק מברדיצ׳ב defended him. Tuberculosis led him to seek treatment in Lviv and finally to move to Uman, where he chose burial near victims of the 1768 massacre and died during Sukkot in 1810. He appointed no dynastic successor; Breslov continued through ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ while retaining ר׳ נחמן as its sole rebbe. His grave became a major pilgrimage center. Much biographical detail derives from insider texts recorded by ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ, so devotional claims are distinguished here from independently datable travel and publication history.
title: מייסד חסידות ברסלב

name: ר׳ נתן שטרנהרץ מברסלב
bio: ר׳ נתן בן ר׳ נפתלי הרץ שטרנהרץ (1780–1844), called ר׳ נתן מנמירוב, ר׳ נתן מברסלב and מוהרנ״ת, was the principal disciple, scribe, editor and disseminator of ר׳ נחמן מברסלב. Raised in a prosperous, learned and initially non-Hasidic Nemyriv family, he studied Talmud and halakhah intensively and married into the family of ר׳ דוד צבי אוירבך. A spiritual search brought him to ר׳ נחמן in Bratslav in 1802. He began recording the master's discourses with exceptional care, helped prepare ליקוטי מוהר״ן, and after ר׳ נחמן's death preserved conversations, biography and tales that otherwise would largely have been lost. He served as Breslov's informal leader but never claimed to be rebbe, maintaining ר׳ נחמן as the movement's sole master. He established the annual Rosh Hashanah gathering at Uman, traveled widely to strengthen small communities, undertook a hazardous pilgrimage to the Land of Israel in 1822, acquired a printing press and devoted his life to publication. His own major works—especially ליקוטי הלכות and ליקוטי תפילות—creatively apply Breslov teaching to halakhah, prayer and daily religious life rather than merely transcribing his teacher. During the anti-Breslov campaign led by ר׳ משה צבי מסאווראן, he endured denunciation, arrest, restrictions and temporary exile from Bratslav. He returned, rebuilt the weakened community and died in Bratslav in 1844. Because much detailed chronology derives from his sacred autobiography and internal Breslov sources, this record distinguishes firsthand testimony, later communal memory and independently documented publication history.
title: מוהרנ״ת

name: Yaakov Tzvi Mecklenburg
bio: Ashkenazi rabbi and scholar, best known as the author of the Torah commentary Haketav Vehakkabbalah. Served as Rabbi of Königsberg for over 30 years and a staunch opponent of Reform Judaism.

name: Yehuda Aryeh Leon Bibas
bio: Sephardic rabbi, physician, Chief Rabbi of Corfu, and prominent forerunner of modern Zionism.

name: ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון (הרש״ש)
bio: ר׳ שמואל בן יוסף שטראשון (1793–1872), universally known in the Talmudic world as הרש״ש, was a Vilna merchant, communal leader and exceptionally wide-ranging Talmudist whose concise glosses became a standard companion to the Babylonian Talmud. He must not be confused with the eighteenth-century Jerusalem kabbalist ר׳ שלום שרעבי, who is also called הרש״ש. Born in Zaskevichi in the former Vilna region, he was first educated by his father, ר׳ יוסף, and descended from a learned rabbinic family. At about thirteen he married Sarah, daughter of the merchant ר׳ דוד שטראשון, moved to his wife's family near Vilna and adopted their surname; before that he was known as Zaskovitzer after his birthplace. In the intellectual world surrounding his father-in-law's study house he learned from ר׳ אברהם דנציג, author of חיי אדם, who cited the young scholar under his original surname. After Napoleon's army destroyed the family distillery during the 1812 invasion, the household relocated to Vilna. Commercial support—managed principally by his wife and later other relatives—allowed him to devote most of his life to study, teaching and public service. He gave well-attended daily Talmud lectures without payment, notably in the synagogue on Popławska Street, and the arguments developed in that setting fed the penetrating textual notes now called הגהות הרש״ש. His method joined traditional Lithuanian lomdut to precise textual criticism and a striking command of Hebrew grammar, history, geography and languages. In 1827 he participated in establishing the short-lived Yeshivat ha-Arba'im, and he became one of Vilna's most respected communal figures. He corresponded with leading scholars, supported charitable activity including interest-free assistance, and declined an invitation to become rabbi of Suwałki because he preferred independent study and teaching. His notes cover almost every tractate of Mishnah and Talmud, regularly proposing emendations or resolving difficulties through parallels elsewhere in rabbinic literature. He also annotated Midrash Rabbah, Shulchan Arukh and the Mishneh Torah of ר׳ משה בן מימון. Although later editions made his surname—and the acronym הרש״ש—familiar wherever the Vilna Talmud was studied, much of his writing remained embedded in margins, other scholars' books and posthumous compilations rather than in a single systematic treatise. No authenticated portrait of ר׳ שמואל was located in Wikimedia Commons, Wikipedia, YIVO or the National Library searches; commonly reproduced Strashun portraits depict his son ר׳ מתתיהו שטראשון and are therefore deliberately excluded.
title: הרש״ש מווילנה

name: Zvi Hirsch Kalischer
bio: Orthodox German rabbi and early proto-Zionist thinker, best known for his book 'Derishat Tzion' (1862), which called for Jewish resettlement in the Land of Israel through natural means, agriculture, and colonization societies. His influence paved the way for modern Zionism.

name: Samuel David Luzzatto (Shadal)
bio: Italian-Austrian Jewish scholar, poet, Bible exegete, and member of the Wissenschaft des Judentums. Professor at Padua, prolific writer, and defender of traditional Judaism against philosophical and rationalist approaches.

name: Nathan Marcus HaKohen Adler
bio: Chief Rabbi of the British Empire (1845–1890). First university-educated Chief Rabbi, known for unifying Anglo-Jewry and founding the United Synagogue.

name: ר׳ שלמה גאנצפריד
bio: ר׳ שלמה בן ר׳ יוסף גאנצפריד (1804–1886), universally associated with קיצור שולחן ערוך, was a Hungarian Orthodox rabbi, dayan, posek and exceptionally influential author of practical halakhah. Born in Ungvár—today Uzhhorod, Ukraine—he was orphaned at eight and raised under the guardianship of ר׳ צבי הירש הלר, the city’s rabbi and rosh yeshiva. At about fifteen he followed his teacher to Bonyhád and studied there for nearly a decade before ordination and marriage. He briefly attempted commerce, including the wine trade, but in 1830 accepted the rabbinate of Brezovica. In 1849 he returned to Ungvár as a dayan, serving alongside ר׳ מאיר אייזנשטטר (מהר״ם אַ״ש) and remaining on the rabbinical court until his death. Confronted by the religious transformations and Orthodox–Neolog conflicts of nineteenth-century Hungary, he concluded that ordinary Jews needed a lucid, usable command of daily law. His קיצור שולחן ערוך, first printed at Ungvár in 1864, distilled practical rulings concerning prayer, blessings, food, Shabbat, festivals, business, marriage, mourning and other areas into concise Hebrew. It spread rapidly through Hebrew, Yiddish and many translations and became a formative household and school manual for Ashkenazi Jewry. Earlier, his קסת הסופר had systematized the laws of writing Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot and received the endorsement of ר׳ משה סופר. His other books addressed Talmud, shechita, family purity, divorce documents and biblical interpretation. At the 1869 Jewish Congress in Budapest he became a prominent spokesman for Hungarian Orthodoxy. He died in Ungvár on 30 July 1886.
title: בעל קיצור שולחן ערוך

name: ר׳ צבי הירש חיות
bio: ר׳ צבי הירש חיות (1805–1855), known as מהר״ץ חיות, was a Galician rabbi, Talmudist, halakhist, and historical scholar who sought to combine fidelity to rabbinic authority with disciplined investigation of the development of the Oral Torah. Born into a wealthy scholarly family in Brody, he studied under Galician authorities including ר׳ אפרים זלמן מרגליות and acquired broad linguistic and secular learning. He maintained important intellectual relationships with ר׳ נחמן קרוכמל and ר׳ שלמה יהודה רפפורט, though their views and personal relations did not always coincide. Appointed district rabbi of Żółkiew in 1829, he served there for more than twenty years. In response to Austrian regulations, he passed external examinations at the University of Lwów in 1846 and received official authorization to continue in the rabbinate—not, as sometimes claimed, a doctorate. His studies addressed rabbinic hermeneutics, the formation of the Talmuds and Midrashim, legal authority, communal enactments, textual criticism, and the boundary between tradition and historical scholarship. He opposed the Reform rabbinical conferences while also criticizing intellectual isolation within Orthodoxy. Elected rabbi of Kalisz in 1852, he encountered local opposition and remained three years. Illness brought him back to Galicia in 1855, and he died in Lwów. His הגהות מהר״ץ חיות became a standard feature of the Vilna Talmud.
title: מהר״ץ חיות

name: שמשון רפאל הירש (Samson Raphael Hirsch)
bio: German Orthodox rabbi (1808–1888). Intellectual founder of the Torah im Derech Eretz approach, which emphasized combining Torah observance with worldly involvement. Served as rabbi in Oldenburg, Emden, and Nikolsburg, and from 1851 led the secessionist Orthodox community in Frankfurt am Main. Vocal opponent of Reform and proto-Zionism. Author of Nineteen Letters, Horeb, and extensive Torah commentary.

name: ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (המלבי״ם)
bio: ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל וייזר (1809–1879), universally known by the acronym המלבי״ם, was a rabbi, halakhist, Hebrew grammarian, preacher and one of the nineteenth century’s most systematic Jewish biblical commentators. Born in Volochysk, Volhynia, he was orphaned young and educated by his father, his stepfather ר׳ לייב מוולוצ'יסק and ר׳ משה הלוי הורוויץ; he later studied in Warsaw and with ר׳ צבי הירש אייכנשטיין מזידיטשוב. After promoting his first halakhic work across Europe, he served communities in Wreschen and Kempen and became known as the Kempener Maggid. As chief rabbi of Bucharest he strengthened kashrut, education, Hebrew printing and the eruv, but his opposition to religious reform and conflicts with communal elites led to arrest and expulsion in 1864. Thereafter he moved through Ruse, Istanbul, Paris, Łęczyca, Kherson, Mogilev and Königsberg, repeatedly encountering political or communal opposition. His התורה והמצוה argued through detailed linguistic rules that rabbinic halakhic interpretation is rooted precisely in the biblical text; מקראי קודש applied his distinction between verbal explanation and contextual interpretation across most of the Prophets and Writings. While traveling to accept the Kremenchuk rabbinate, he became ill and died in Kyiv on Rosh Hashanah 5640.
title: המלבי״ם
aliases: Meir Leibush ben Yechiel Michel Wisser
ר׳ מאיר ליבוש בן יחיאל מיכל

name: Yisrael Salanter
bio: Rabbi Yisrael ben Ze'ev Wolf Lipkin (1809–1883), known as Yisrael Salanter, was the founder of the Musar Movement, a leading Rosh Yeshiva, and a Talmudist. He emphasized ethical refinement and self-discipline as central to Jewish life, inspiring generations through his teachings and disciples.

name: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט
bio: ר׳ אברהם צבי הירש אייזנשטט (probably 1812–21 August 1868), commonly identified by his work פתחי תשובה, was a rabbi and halakhic compiler in the western Russian Empire. Born in Białystok to ר׳ יעקב אשר אייזנשטט and Rachel, he descended from ר׳ מאיר אייזנשטט, author of פנים מאירות. After marrying Yenta Reizel, he continued studying while she operated a stationery business. The family later followed government offices to Grodno; when the business failed there, he became a dayan. He served as rabbi of Bristovitz from 1836 and of Utena from 1856. His פתחי תשובה arranged concise conclusions and references from a vast responsa literature according to the sections of שולחן ערוך. The Yoreh De'ah volume appeared in Vilna in 1836, Even HaEzer during his lifetime, and Choshen Mishpat posthumously. His accompanying נחלת צבי supplied original discussions rather than bibliographic abstracts. Seriously ill in his final year, he travelled from Utena to Königsberg for treatment, died there on 3 Elul 5628 and was buried in the local Jewish cemetery. פתחי תשובה subsequently became a standard commentary printed alongside שולחן ערוך.
base_name: Avraham Tzvi Hirsch Eisenstadt, author of Pitchei Teshuvah
title: בעל פתחי תשובה

name: ר׳ עבדאללה סומך
bio: ר׳ עבדאללה סומך (1813–13 September 1889), whose fuller Hebrew name was ר׳ עובדיה אברהם יוסף סומך, was the leading educator and a major halakhic authority of nineteenth-century Baghdad. Born there to ר׳ אברהם יוסף יחזקאל and Khatun, he traced his family to ר׳ נסים גאון. He studied under ר׳ יעקב בר יוסף הרופא, who called him his outstanding and discerning pupil, and also learned from ר׳ משה חיים. After marriage to Sarah he initially worked successfully in commerce. Concerned by declining advanced Torah study, he left business and taught a small group without payment. With patron Ezekiel Reuben Manasseh, this circle became Midrash Abu Menashi in 1840 and later the renowned Midrash Beit Zilkha, which he headed until his death. His students included ר׳ יוסף חיים, ר׳ אליהו מני, ר׳ אברהם הלל, ר׳ יצחק מג׳לד, ר׳ ששון שמוחה and many later leaders of Iraqi Jewry. Communities across Iraq, Persia, India and Central Asia sent him legal questions; surviving responsa show engagement with technological and social change as well as ritual law. His best-known work, זבחי צדק, systematized practical rulings and Baghdadi custom on Yoreh De'ah, especially shechita and treifot. It appeared posthumously, so its printing place must not be mistaken for a movement in his lifetime. During Baghdad's 1889 cholera epidemic he became ill near the city and died after being brought home. Conflict over his first burial caused arrests and anti-Jewish violence; about three months later Ottoman authorities permitted reburial in Baghdad's Jewish cemetery. His school and rulings helped connect Baghdad's rabbinic centre with the expanding Baghdadi diaspora throughout Asia.
title: בעל זבחי צדק, ראש מדרש בית זלכה ופוסק יהדות בבל

name: Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (Netziv)
bio: Rabbi Naftali Zvi Yehuda Berlin (1816–1893), known as the Netziv, was Rosh Yeshiva of Volozhin for 40 years, a leading Torah scholar, author of Haamek Davar, Haamek She'elah, and Meishiv Davar, and an early supporter of Chovevei Zion.

name: Yitzchak Elchanan Spektor
bio: Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan Spektor (1817–1896) was the Chief Rabbi of Kovno, one of the leading halachic authorities of the 19th century, renowned for his responsa, his leadership during crises, and his moderation toward modern movements while remaining firmly Orthodox.

name: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יוסף דובער הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (c.1820–1 May 1892), known as the בית הלוי, was a Lithuanian Talmudist, communal rabbi and the first major rabbinic leader of the Brisk branch of the Soloveitchik family. Born in Nesvizh to ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and Rivka, a descendant of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין, he studied at Volozhin and taught in Minsk while still young. In 1854 he joined ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין in leading the Volozhin Yeshiva, where his dialectical, conceptual approach helped prepare the ground for the later Brisker method developed by his son ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. He became rabbi of Slutsk in 1865, established advanced study there and was remembered for organized assistance to poor children. Conflict with communal modernizers led him to resign and live in Warsaw under difficult financial circumstances. After ר׳ יהושע לייב דיסקין left Brisk, ר׳ יוסף דוב accepted that city’s rabbinate around 1878–1879 and served until his death. His responsa בית הלוי address all four sections of Shulchan Aruch and combine close textual analysis with practical communal judgment. בית הלוי על התורה preserves discourses on Genesis, part of Exodus and festival themes. His students included ר׳ יוסף רוזין and ר׳ זלמן סנדר שפירא; his son ר׳ חיים succeeded him in Brisk.
title: בעל בית הלוי; רבה של בריסק

name: ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין
bio: ר׳ צדוק בן ר׳ יעקב הכהן רבינוביץ (1823–1900), known as ר׳ צדוק הכהן מלובלין, was a Hasidic master, Talmudist, halakhist, kabbalist and unusually wide-ranging religious thinker. Born in Kreuzburg in Courland to a Lithuanian rabbinic family, he was orphaned young and raised by his uncle ר׳ יוסף בן אשר, a student of ר׳ חיים מוולוז׳ין. His early formation was learned and non-Hasidic. A marital crisis led him to travel through Poland seeking the exceptional authorization of one hundred rabbis for divorce; the precise route is imperfectly preserved. During those journeys he encountered Hasidism and became a disciple of ר׳ מרדכי יוסף ליינר מאיזביצה. After his teacher's death in 1854, he supported his friend ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר as leader of the Lublin circle and spent more than three decades in study, prayer, writing and relative seclusion. Only after ר׳ יהודה לייב איגר died in 1888 did he accept leadership. His thought extends the Izbica concern with divine providence, human will, sin and repentance while developing original accounts of Oral Torah, historical change, imagination, language, psychology, sacred time and the spiritual potential latent in every Jew. He combined extraordinary command of rabbinic and kabbalistic sources with interests extending to astronomy, mathematics and general knowledge. He refused to publish most writings during his lifetime but authorized posthumous publication; many remaining manuscripts were later destroyed in the Lublin ghetto. His surviving books—especially צדקת הצדיק, פרי צדיק, רסיסי לילה and תקנת השבין—became foundational works of modern Hasidic thought and influenced figures including ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר, ר׳ יצחק הוטנר and ר׳ גדליה שור.
title: הכהן מלובלין

name: Aruch HaShulchan
bio: Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein (1829–1908) was a Lithuanian rabbi and posek, best known as the author of 'Aruch HaShulchan', a monumental halakhic work covering all four sections of the Shulchan Aruch. He served as rabbi of Novogrudok for over 34 years, where he was recognized as a leading halakhic authority of his time. He was also the brother-in-law of the Netziv of Volozhin.  https://jsoundbites.podbean.com/e/the-life-legacy-of-the-aruch-hashulchan/

name: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני
bio: ר׳ חיים חזקיהו מדיני (7 Cheshvan 5593–24 Kislev 5665; 1832–1904), commonly called the Sdei Chemed after his encyclopedic halakhic work, was a Jerusalem-born Sephardi rabbi, communal leader and prolific legal scholar. The son of ר׳ רפאל אשר אליהו מדיני and Kalu Vida, he studied in Jerusalem under ר׳ יצחק קובו and ר׳ יוסף נסים בורלא, married Rivka at eighteen and received semikhah while still young. His father's death in 1853 left him responsible for an extended household and prompted relocation to Constantinople, where he taught, lectured and wrote while declining opportunities that would interrupt his study. In 1867 he accepted the rabbinate of Karasubazar—now Bilohirsk—in Crimea. During thirty-two years there he founded schools and yeshivot, issued communal regulations, addressed the distinctive traditions of Krymchak Jewry and maintained an international halakhic correspondence. Most of שדי חמד was assembled there. The work alphabetically synthesizes Talmudic and later legal rules, responsa, bibliographical information and scholarly biographies; its scale made it an important bridge between dispersed rabbinic literature and later Torah encyclopedias. He returned to Jerusalem in 1899. Wishing to avoid nomination as Rishon LeZion, he moved to Hebron in 1901, but after the deaths of ר׳ אליהו מני and ר׳ חיים רחמים יוסף פרנקו he accepted leadership of the community. He taught and completed parts of his work at Beit Romano, died in Hebron in 1904 and was buried in its ancient Jewish cemetery.

name: Yisrael Meir ha-Kohen Kagan (Chofetz Chaim)
bio: Influential halachic authority, ethicist, and founder of the Radin Yeshiva.

name: Hermann Adler HaKohen
bio: Chief Rabbi of the British Empire (1891–1911). Son and successor of Chief Rabbi Nathan Marcus Adler. A defender of modernized orthodoxy, Anglo-Jewish history, and Jewish rights. Remembered for raising the dignity and prominence of the Chief Rabbinate.

name: Meir Simcha HaKohen of Dvinsk
bio: Rabbi Meir Simcha HaKohen of Dvinsk (1843–1926) was one of the leading halachic authorities of his generation. Known as the Ohr Somayach after his magnum opus on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah, he served as Rabbi of the non-Hasidic community of Dvinsk for nearly 40 years. His second major work, Meshech Chochma, offered profound insights on the Torah and addressed contemporary challenges. He supported Religious Zionism after the Balfour Declaration, warning against over-assimilation with his famous phrase about Jews seeing 'Berlin as Jerusalem.' His works remain foundational in Torah study, and the global Ohr Somayach yeshiva network is named in his honor.
title: Rabbi of Dvinsk, author of Ohr Somayach and Meshech Chochma

name: Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter
bio: Rabbi Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter (1847–1905), known as the Sfas Emes, was the second Rebbe of the Ger Hasidic dynasty. Orphaned young and raised by his grandfather the Chiddushei Harim, he became one of the most influential Hasidic leaders of 19th-century Poland. His Torah teachings, collected in the work 'Sfas Emes,' are studied worldwide as classics of Hasidic thought.
title: Second Gerrer Rebbe, author of Sfas Emes

name: ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ
bio: ר׳ יוסף יוזל הורביץ (1847–1919), known as הסבא מנובהרדוק, was one of the most radical institution-builders of the Lithuanian mussar movement. Born in Plungė and educated in the Lithuanian rabbinic world, he married young and entered business in Švėkšna. An encounter in Memel with ר׳ ישראל סלנטר redirected his life toward disciplined ethical self-formation. He studied in Kovno with figures including ר׳ יצחק בלאזר, ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם and ר׳ אברהם שנקר, then pursued prolonged periods of solitude and introspection. Encouraged by ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו to serve the public, he created kollelim and yeshivot across the Russian Empire. The central yeshiva opened at Navahrudak in the 1890s and generated the decentralized Novardok network. Its demanding pedagogy sought freedom from status, fear and social approval through bitachon, rigorous self-examination, communal study and deliberately discomfiting exercises. During the First World War he refused to abandon his students: the displaced movement regrouped in Homel and later expanded around Kyiv. He died there during the 1919 typhus epidemic after attending the sick. His teachings, recorded and edited by disciples as מדרגת האדם, made radical trust in God and the struggle against self-interest the enduring intellectual signature of Novardok. His remains were reinterred at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem in 1963; that posthumous event is not represented as a map movement, so the figure correctly disappears in 1919.
title: הסבא מנובהרדוק

name: R' Chaim HaLevi Soloveitchik (Rav Chaim of Brisk)
bio: Rav Chaim HaLevi Soloveitchik (1853–1918), known as Rav Chaim of Brisk, was one of the greatest rabbinic figures of the 20th century and the father of the Brisker method of Talmudic study. Born in Volozhin to Rabbi Yosef Dov (Beis HaLevi) Soloveitchik and Zirl née Efron, he studied in the Volozhin Yeshiva and later married Lipsha, daughter of Rabbi Raphael Shapira, son-in-law of the Netziv. He became deputy head of the Volozhin Yeshiva at age 27 and later the rabbi of Brisk. He was renowned for his innovative analytical method of learning, his stringency in matters of pikuach nefesh, his fierce opposition to Zionism and the Mussar movement, and his devotion to the poor and needy. His teachings laid the foundation for the Lithuanian yeshiva world, and his legacy was carried forward by his son, Rav Yitzchak Ze'ev Soloveitchik (the Brisker Rav).

name: ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין
bio: ר׳ שמואל בורנשטיין (4 Cheshvan 5616–24 Tevet 5686; 1855–1926), known from his teachings as the שם משמואל, was the second Sochatchover Rebbe and a major interpreter of the Kotsk–Sochatchov tradition. He was born in Kock in the household of his maternal grandfather ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן. His parents were ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין, later author of אבני נזר and founder of the Sochatchov dynasty, and Sarah Tzina Morgenstern. He accompanied his father through successive rabbinates in Parczew, Krośniewice, Nasielsk, and finally Sochaczew, remaining his closest student. In 1891 his father sent him to Ottoman Palestine to investigate purchasing land for an observant agricultural settlement, but Ottoman restrictions frustrated the project.
