After his father’s death in 1910, he succeeded him as rebbe and head of the Sochaczew yeshiva. The First World War destroyed Sochaczew as a functioning Hasidic centre; after wartime detention in Germany he re-established his court in Łódź and then, in 1919, in quieter Zgierz. His discourses combine close biblical and rabbinic interpretation, Kabbalistic structures, Kotsk moral intensity, and teachings received from ר׳ אברהם בורנשטיין and ר׳ מנחם מנדל מורגנשטרן. Collected from manuscripts and students’ copies, they were published posthumously as שם משמואל. He died in the resort town of Otwock and was buried beside his father in Sochaczew.
title: האדמו״ר השני מסוכטשוב; בעל שם משמואל

name: Joseph Rosen
bio: Rabbi Joseph Rosen (1858–1936), known as the Rogatchover Gaon, was one of the most brilliant Talmudic minds of his era. Born in Rogachov into a Chabad-Kapust Hasidic family, he studied under the Beis HaLevi in Slutsk and Rabbi Yehoshua Leib Diskin in Shklov. In 1889 he became rabbi of the Hasidic community of Dvinsk, where he served alongside Rabbi Meir Simcha of Dvinsk. His halachic responsa were concise, cryptic, and deeply rooted in Rambam and early Rishonim, earning him a reputation as a unique genius. He authored an estimated 50,000 responsa and his magnum opus, Tzofnath Paneach, on Rambam’s Mishneh Torah, continues to shape Torah scholarship. Despite persecution, many of his writings were preserved and published after his death. He is remembered as one of the great halachic and philosophical authorities of the modern era.
title: The Rogatchover Gaon, author of Tzofnath Paneach

name: Rabbi Baruch HaLevi Epstein
bio: Rabbi Baruch HaLevi Epstein (1860–1942) was a Lithuanian rabbi and scholar, son of Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein, author of the Aruch HaShulchan, and Michla, sister of the Netziv of Volozhin. He is best known as the author of Torah Temimah, a classic commentary that connects the Written Torah with the Oral Torah. He was educated at the Volozhin Yeshiva, ordained by leading rabbis including his uncle the Netziv and Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik, and later studied in Vienna. Though he worked for many years as a banker in Pinsk, he continued intensive Torah study and writing. He was active in the Zion Association for Hebrew language revival, and his correspondence during the Beilis blood libel trial defending the Jewish people was widely publicized. He traveled to the United States between 1923 and 1926 to publish his works. He refused rabbinical positions in Pinsk, St. Petersburg, and Moscow, preferring to focus on scholarship. He died in the Holocaust in 1942 in Pinsk and was buried in Karlin.

name: Rabbi Shimon Yehuda Shkop
bio: Rabbi Shimon Yehuda Shkop (1860–1939) was a leading Lithuanian Rosh Yeshiva and Talmudic innovator. Born in Torez, Ukraine, he studied in Mir and later in Volozhin under the Netziv, also joining Rav Chaim Soloveitchik’s chaburah. In 1884 he became rosh mesivta in Telz, shaping the 'Telz derech' in learning, a method of clarity and analysis. After rabbinic posts in Malech and Bransk, he was appointed Rosh Yeshiva of Sha'ar HaTorah in Grodno in 1920, where he taught thousands of students. In 1928 he visited the U.S., lecturing at Yeshiva University and briefly serving as Rosh Yeshiva at RIETS before returning to Grodno. His magnum opus 'Sha'arei Yosher' remains a classic of lomdus. He died in Grodno in 1939 as the Russian army advanced, leaving a legacy as one of the great Torah educators of his era.
title: Rosh Yeshiva of Telz and later Sha'ar HaTorah in Grodno

name: Sholom Dovber Schneersohn
bio: Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (1860–1920), known as the Rebbe Rashab, was the fifth Rebbe of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. Born in Lubavitch to Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Maharash, he became one of the most influential Chassidic leaders of the late Russian Empire. He formally assumed leadership of Chabad in 1892 and transformed the movement through profound Chassidic teachings, organized communal activism, and the founding of the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva system. During World War I he relocated from Lubavitch to Rostov-on-Don, where he continued leading Chabad under increasingly difficult political conditions. His teachings became foundational to modern Chabad philosophy and education.

name: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz
bio: Rabbi Baruch Dov (Ber) Leibowitz (1862–1939) was a leading disciple of Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik of Brisk and later rosh yeshiva of the Kamenitz Yeshiva. He was renowned for his brilliant analytical Talmudic methodology and his sefer Birkat Shmuel. His yeshiva in Kamenitz became one of the great centers of Torah learning in pre-war Eastern Europe.

name: ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי
bio: ר׳ חיים עוזר גרודזינסקי (24 August 1863–9 August 1940) was a Lithuanian posek, av beit din and communal leader whose Vilna office became a clearing-house for halakhic questions, institutional policy and relief across Eastern European Orthodox Jewry. Born in Iwye to ר׳ דוד שלמה גרודזינסקי, the town’s rabbi, he studied among the perushim of Eishyshok and at Volozhin, where ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק influenced his analytical learning. After marrying Leah, daughter of Vilna dayan ר׳ אליהו אליעזר גרודזינסקי, he joined the Vilna beit din in 1887. He never held an uncontested title of ‘chief rabbi of Vilna’; rather, his authority grew through the rabbinical court, scholarship and communal trust. He supported the Ramailes yeshiva, taught an elite scholars’ group and answered correspondents internationally. At Agudath Israel’s 1912 founding conference he entered its leading rabbinic council, while retaining an independent Lithuanian leadership role. After the First World War he and ר׳ ישראל מאיר הכהן organized support for devastated yeshivot; the Vaad Hayeshivot, founded in 1924, coordinated fundraising and material aid for a large regional network. His three-volume שו״ת אחיעזר, published in Vilna between 1922 and 1939, addresses all sections of the Shulchan Aruch and modern communal problems with conceptual precision and practical responsibility. He also advocated for persecuted German Jews after 1933. When war divided Poland in 1939, he urged displaced yeshivot toward temporarily Lithuanian Vilna and organized assistance for thousands of refugees. He died before Soviet repression and Nazi mass murder destroyed the institutional world he had laboured to sustain.
title: בעל שו״ת אחיעזר, אב בית הדין וממנהיגי יהדות וילנה

name: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק
bio: ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק (7 September 1865–1 September 1935), known as Rav Kook or הראי״ה קוק, was a halakhist, mystic, Hebrew thinker and formative religious-Zionist leader. Born in Grīva beside Dvinsk to ר׳ שלמה זלמן קוק and Perel Zlata Felman, he combined Lithuanian yeshivah learning with Hasidic and kabbalistic traditions. He studied at Volozhin under ר׳ נפתלי צבי יהודה ברלין and served the communities of Žeimelis and Bauska. In 1904 he became rabbi of Jaffa and the surrounding agricultural settlements, addressing the practical religious questions of renewed Jewish life in the Land of Israel. Stranded in Europe during the First World War, he lived in St Gallen and then led London’s Machzike Hadath congregation. Returning in 1919, he became Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Jerusalem; in 1921 he helped establish the Chief Rabbinate and became the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandatory Palestine. He founded Mercaz HaRav in 1924. His writings—including אורות, אורות התשובה, עין איה, שבת הארץ and responsa—joined halakhah, spirituality, national rebirth and universal ethics. Many works were edited posthumously by his son ר׳ צבי יהודה הכהן קוק and students including ר׳ דוד כהן and ר׳ יעקב משה חרל״פ.
title: הראי״ה קוק; הרב הראשי האשכנזי הראשון לארץ ישראל

name: ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר (Imrei Emes)
bio: Rav Avraham Mordechai Alter (1866–1948), known as the Imrei Emes after his Torah work, was the third Rebbe of Ger and one of the most influential Hasidic leaders of the 20th century. Under his leadership, Ger became the largest Hasidic dynasty in prewar Poland, with tens of thousands of followers. He rebuilt Ger after the Holocaust in Eretz Yisrael, continuing his dynasty's influence.

name: Chaim Elazar Spira
bio: Rabbi Chaim Elazar Spira (1868–1937) was the Rebbe of the Munkacs Hasidic dynasty and a leading rabbinic authority in interwar Europe. Author of the monumental halachic work 'Minchas Elazar', he was renowned for his sharp style, uncompromising positions, and strong opposition to Zionism and Agudath Israel. He built major Torah institutions in Munkács, including the Darchei Teshuva yeshiva and Machzike Torah schools. His leadership culminated in the famous 1933 wedding of his only daughter, attended by tens of thousands. Though he passed away in 1937, the Munkacs dynasty continues today, led by his grandson Rabbi Moshe Leib Rabinovich from Brooklyn.
title: Rebbe of the Munkacs Hasidic dynasty, author of Minchas Elazar

name: איסר זלמן מלצר (Isser Zalman Meltzer)
bio: Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer (1870–1953) was a leading Lithuanian Torah scholar and Rosh Yeshiva, author of the classic halachic work Even HaEzel. He studied in Volozhin and under Rav Chaim Soloveitchik, later serving as Rosh Yeshiva in Slutsk. After immigrating to Eretz Yisrael, he became head of the Etz Chaim Yeshiva in Jerusalem. Teacher and mentor to many future Torah leaders, including his son-in-law Rav Aharon Kotler.

name: R'Moshe Rosen
bio: R'Moshe Rosen.
title: Chief Rabbi of Romania

name: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר
bio: ר׳ יעקב חיים סופר (c. 1870–27 May 1939), generally known as בעל כף החיים, was an Iraqi-born Sephardi halakhist and kabbalist whose encyclopedic commentary became a major guide to practical law and custom. Born in Baghdad to ר׳ יצחק ברוך סופר and Esther, he studied at the Beit Zilkha yeshivah under ר׳ עבדאללה סומך and absorbed the teaching and communal traditions of ר׳ יוסף חיים, the Ben Ish Chai. His formation joined rigorous halakhic learning, Iraqi minhag and Lurianic Kabbalah. In 1904 he travelled to Ottoman Palestine with Iraqi colleagues, visited sacred sites and chose to remain in Jerusalem. He first joined the kabbalistic circle of Beit El in the Old City and also studied among the Rehovot HaNahar kabbalists associated with ר׳ חיים שאול דוויק הכהן. By 1909 he was teaching at Shoshanim LeDavid, the Iraqi synagogue and yeshivah in the Beit Israel–Bukharan area, where he spent the rest of his scholarly career and served the Babylonian community. There he composed כף החיים, arranged according to Shulchan Aruch. Its eight author-published volumes on Orach Chayim appeared from 1910 to 1933, followed by the first Yoreh De'ah volume in 1936. The work gathers an unusually broad range of Rishonim, Acharonim, local customs and kabbalistic rulings, especially those associated with ר׳ יצחק לוריא, while normally identifying its sources. It consequently became particularly influential in Sephardi and Mizrahi halakhic practice. He also wrote קול יעקב on scribal law, יגל יעקב, ישמח ישראל and חיים עד העולם. ר׳ יעקב חיים died in Jerusalem on 9 Sivan 5699 and was buried on the Mount of Olives. A second Yoreh De'ah volume was issued posthumously from his manuscript and completed by ר׳ עובדיה יוסף; it must therefore not be represented as wholly finished by the author himself.
title: בעל כף החיים, פוסק ומקובל

name: Joseph Herman Hertz
bio: Chief Rabbi of the British Empire (1913–1946). A biblical scholar, eloquent preacher, and vigorous defender of Orthodoxy and Zionism. Guided Anglo-Jewry through both World Wars and the Holocaust. Known for his Torah commentary and his global 'Imperial tour' of Jewish communities.

name: Elchonon Bunim Wasserman
bio: Rabbi Elchonon Bunim Wasserman (1874–1941) was one of the foremost disciples of the Chofetz Chaim and a leading Torah educator of prewar Europe. Born in Biržai, Lithuania, he studied at Telshe, Brisk under Rav Chaim Soloveitchik, and later in Radin with the Chofetz Chaim. In 1921 he became Rosh Yeshiva of Ohel Torah-Baranovich, raising generations of talmidim with his clarity in learning and steadfast faith. He traveled to America to raise funds but returned to Poland before the war to remain with his students. In 1941 he was martyred in Kaunas together with other rabbis, urging his followers to accept their fate as korbanot for Klal Yisrael. His writings and students carried on his legacy, securing his place as a spiritual heir to the Chofetz Chaim.
title: Rosh Yeshiva of Ohel Torah-Baranovich, disciple of the Chofetz Chaim

name: ירוחם ליבוביץ (Yerucham Levovitz)
bio: Rabbi Yerucham Levovitz (1875–1936) was the mashgiach ruchani of the Mir Yeshiva in Poland. A foremost disciple of the Alter of Kelm, he transmitted the Mussar tradition with depth, discipline, and clarity. His influence shaped generations of Mirrer talmidim, and his teachings are preserved in the multi-volume 'Daas Torah'.

name: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן
bio: ר׳ אליהו לופיאן (1876–21 September 1970), widely called ר׳ אלי׳, was one of the twentieth century's most influential transmitters of the Kelm school of Mussar. Born in Grajewo to Yaakov and Frida Lopian, he remained in Łomża to study when his family emigrated to the United States, then entered the Kelm Talmud Torah and learned under ר׳ שמחה זיסל זיו and ר׳ יצחק בלאזר. He married Sarah Leah, daughter of ר׳ יצחק דוד רוטמן, and became a central teacher and institutional leader in Kelm. During the First World War he remained with students and continued teaching; afterward he traveled through Lithuanian communities encouraging students to return and helped rebuild the yeshiva. In the later 1920s he settled in London and served at Etz Chaim Yeshiva in the East End alongside ר׳ נחמן שלמה גרינשפן, shaping generations of British rabbinic students. He immigrated to Israel in 1950, taught Mussar in Jerusalem, and in 1951 became the spiritual director of Knesses Chizkiyahu, first at Zikhron Ya'akov and from 1955 at Kfar Hasidim. His demanding Kelm discipline was joined to close personal concern for students. His talks were edited posthumously by his student ר׳ שלום מרדכי הכהן שבדרון as לב אליהו, an enduring anthology of Torah interpretation, faith and ethical self-examination. He died in Jerusalem on 20 Elul 5730 and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: מבעלי המוסר של קלם ומשגיח ישיבת כנסת חזקיהו

name: R' Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz
bio: Rabbi Avraham Yeshaya Karelitz (1878–1953), known as the Chazon Ish after his magnum opus, was the leading Haredi authority in Eretz Yisrael during the mid-20th century. Born in Kossow, Poland, he became renowned in Europe for his penetrating Torah works though he held no official rabbinic post. In 1933, he immigrated to Bnei Brak, where he quickly became the undisputed halachic and spiritual leader of the Yishuv’s Haredi community. He guided religious policy on issues such as army service, medicine, agriculture (including Shemitta), and yeshiva life, and laid the foundations for the modern Torah community in Israel. His home became a center of guidance for rabbis, doctors, and politicians alike.
title: Chazon Ish

name: Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Finkel
bio: Rabbi Hezekiah Eliezer Yehuda Finkel (1879–1965) was the Rosh Yeshiva of the Mir Yeshiva in Poland and later its re-establishment in Eretz Yisrael. Born in Kelm to Gittel and Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel (the Alter of Slabodka), he studied in Telz under Rabbi Eliezer Gordon and Rabbi Shimon Shkop, in Brisk under Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik, and in many other yeshivot. In 1897 he was among the group of students sent by his father to strengthen the Slutsk Yeshiva under the Ridvaz. He later studied in Mir, where he married Malka, daughter of Rabbi Eliyahu Baruch Kamai, and eventually succeeded his father-in-law as Rosh Yeshiva. During World War I he led the yeshiva in exile to Ukraine, and after World War II reestablished the Mir in Jerusalem. He served as a member of the Council of Torah Sages of Agudat Yisrael and was renowned for his scholarship, leadership, and piety. After losing family in the Holocaust, he abstained from eating meat for the last 25 years of his life. He passed away in 1965 and was buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.

name: Rabbi Moshe Soloveichik
bio: Rabbi Moshe Soloveichik (1879–1941) was an Orthodox rabbi and Rosh Yeshiva at the Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary (RIETS) of Yeshiva University. Born in Volozhin as the middle son of Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik and grandson of the Beis HaLevi, he married Pesya Feinstein, daughter of Rabbi Eliyahu Feinstein of Pruzany. He served as rabbi of Raseiniai and later Khislavichi, and was director of Talmud studies at Tachkemoni Seminary in Warsaw. In 1929 he immigrated to New York, joining the faculty of RIETS as Rosh Yeshiva. He was the father of Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik, Rabbi Ahron Soloveichik, and Professor Samuel Soloveichik, and grandfather to a generation of Soloveitchik scholars and leaders.

name: ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר
bio: ר׳ צבי הירש פרבר (approximately 1878/79–1966) was a Lithuanian-born British rabbi, halakhist, preacher and exceptionally prolific Hebrew author. Born in Slabodka, adjoining Kovno, to ר׳ שמעון יהודה ליב פרבר and חנה דבורה, he was formed in the Lithuanian mussar and yeshiva world. Sources associate his education with the Slabodka yeshiva and with ר׳ יצחק אלחנן ספקטור, ר׳ יצחק בלאזר and ר׳ נפתלי אמסטרדם. He migrated to England in 1910 or 1911. In Manchester he taught Talmud and helped establish or lead a yeshiva before moving to London. In July 1913 he became rabbi of the West End Talmud Torah Synagogue in Soho, later commonly called the West End Great Synagogue, and served the congregation for more than forty years, retiring in 1954 or 1955. The congregation and its affiliated burial arrangements gave him an unusual degree of independence from Britain's central religious establishment. He became known as an eloquent Lithuanian-style maggid and a leading representative of immigrant Orthodoxy. He established or helped organize the Committee of Orthodox Rabbis, served in leadership of the London Vaad Harabonim and the Hisachdus Harabonim, supported yeshiva education, and worked on shechita, burial and other communal questions. During ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק's First World War residence in London the two rabbis formed a close friendship, documented by surviving correspondence. ר׳ צבי הירש was also a persistent scholar: accounts place him regularly in the British Museum's Oriental Reading Room, and surviving autograph notebooks confirm sustained work on Torah, Talmud, halakhah and homiletics. His principal publication was כרם הצבי, a multi-volume halakhic and aggadic commentary on the Torah issued between 1920 and 1938; he later published a Passover Haggadah under the same title. His many other books and pamphlets addressed festivals, prayer, Pirkei Avot, King David, Jewish thought and practical legal controversies. He died in London in November 1966. Because celebratory rabbinic accounts sometimes differ over exact dates and offices, this record gives priority to Encyclopaedia Judaica, institutional catalogues, archival evidence and surviving manuscripts, while marking unresolved variants explicitly.
title: רב, דרשן, פוסק ומחבר בלונדון
aliases: צבי הירש בן שמעון יהודה ליב פרבר

name: R'Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn
bio: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (1880–1950), known as the Frierdiker Rebbe or Rayatz, was the sixth Rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch. Born in Lyubavichi as the only son of Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn, he became his father’s secretary at age 15 and soon took on leadership responsibilities. He headed the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva network and advocated for Jewish rights across Russia and Europe. Arrested multiple times under the Czar and again by the Soviets in 1927, his death sentence was commuted after international protest, and he settled in Riga and later Warsaw. In 1940 he was miraculously rescued from Nazi-occupied Warsaw and brought to New York, where he declared 'America is no different' and rebuilt Chabad’s institutions. He founded Kfar Chabad in Israel and laid the groundwork for the global Chabad movement. He passed away in 1950 in Brooklyn and was succeeded by his son-in-law, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe.
title: Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe (Rayatz, Frierdiker Rebbe)

name: ר׳ יחיאל יעקב וויינברג (Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg)
bio: Rabbi Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg (1884–1966), known as the Seridei Eish, was a leading 20th-century halachic authority and Rosh Yeshiva of the Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin. A disciple of Slabodka, he combined Lithuanian yeshiva rigor with modern scholarship. Surviving the Holocaust, he became a central posek for post-war Jewry, especially in matters of modernity, education, and Jewish life in Europe.

name: ר׳ אריה לוין
bio: ר׳ אריה לוין (22 March 1885–28 March 1969) was a Jerusalem educator and pastoral rabbi remembered as רב האסירים, 'the Rabbi/Father of the Prisoners,' and הצדיק הירושלמי. He was born in Orla near Białystok, then in the Russian Empire and now in Poland, to Binyamin Beinush, a forester, and Ethel. His youth was shaped by poverty and persistent travel in search of Torah education. He studied in Slutsk, Slonim, Brest and Pinsk and, after initially being refused admission to Volozhin because of his age, learned in Hlyusk under ר׳ ברוך דב ליבוביץ. He was later accepted at the Volozhin yeshivah and studied under ר׳ רפאל שפירא. These stages formed his Lithuanian yeshivah background, although the precise year of every move is not firmly documented. In 1905 he immigrated alone to Ottoman Palestine, landed at Jaffa and shortly afterward moved to Jerusalem. In Jaffa he met ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק, then rabbi of Jaffa and the surrounding settlements, beginning a close lifelong relationship. In Jerusalem he studied at Yeshivat Torat Chaim and married Tzipora Chana, daughter of ר׳ דוד שפירא. He received rabbinic ordination in 1909 from ר׳ חיים ברלין, ר׳ שמואל סלנט and ר׳ אברהם יצחק הכהן קוק. During the deprivation of the First World War, the family endured severe hunger and lost two daughters. From 1917 until the end of his life, ר׳ אריה served as mashgiaḥ and spiritual educator at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah in Jerusalem. He lived simply, worked closely with children from poor families and resisted attempts to improve his own material circumstances. After ר׳ שלמה אלישיב, author of לשם שבו ואחלמה, immigrated to Jerusalem, ר׳ אריה became his student. His public reputation, however, grew chiefly from sustained acts of pastoral care rather than formal publication or high office. He regularly visited Jerusalem hospitals and deliberately entered institutions whose patients were otherwise socially isolated, including the leprosy hospitals in Talbiya and Bethlehem. He began visiting Jewish criminal prisoners during the British Mandate and continued for roughly twenty-five years. Every Sabbath and festival he walked to the Central Prison in Jerusalem's Russian Compound, prayed with inmates, listened to them, wrote letters and carried messages between prisoners and their families. As underground activists from the Haganah, Irgun and Lehi were imprisoned, he became their trusted spiritual advocate, without limiting his compassion to a single political camp or to political prisoners. His care for condemned underground fighters and other inmates earned the titles רב האסירים and אבי האסירים. Ministry of Defense museum displays preserve this role as part of the history of the Mandate prison. After the 1948 war, he continued visiting prisoners under the new state. In 1949, when the remains of the thirty-five members of the Lamed-Heh convoy were brought for burial and twelve could not be conventionally distinguished, Jerusalem's chief rabbi ר׳ צבי פסח פרנק asked him to conduct the traditional גורל הגר״א procedure. The resulting identifications were accepted by the families and state institutions. This episode belongs to Israeli religious memory; it should be described as a ritual identification accepted at the time, not as a modern forensic method. After independence he established Yeshivat Beit Aryeh in the courtyard of his modest home and appointed his son-in-law ר׳ אליעזר פלצינסקי as its head. He continued work at Etz Chaim, prison and hospital visits, private mediation and support for the poor. Shortly before his death he received the Fighters of the State decoration for assistance rendered during the underground period. He died at Hadassah Medical Center on Friday, 28 March 1969, immediately before Shabbat HaGadol, and was buried that afternoon in Sanhedria Cemetery. The timing fulfilled his request that no eulogies be delivered. His gravestone asks visitors to affirm belief in the resurrection of the dead. Much of the popular memory of ר׳ אריה comes through stories collected by his associate Simcha Raz in איש צדיק היה and צדיק יסוד עולם. These works preserve testimony and shaped his public image, but individual anecdotes require source criticism and should not all be treated as independently verified transcripts. His durable historical significance lies in an unusually inclusive model of rabbinic care that joined Lithuanian learning, Jerusalem education and practical solidarity with prisoners, patients, bereaved families and the poor across religious and political divisions.
title: רב האסירים והצדיק הירושלמי

name: יחזקאל אברמסקי
bio: Rabbi Yechezkel Abramsky (1886–1976) was one of the foremost Torah scholars and halachic authorities of the 20th century. Born in Dashkovichy in the Russian Empire (now Belarus), he studied in Novardok, Telz, Vilna, and Brisk under leading Lithuanian roshei yeshiva including Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski and Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik. He served as rabbi in several Russian communities before becoming chief rabbi of Slutsk. Under Soviet persecution he was arrested, imprisoned, and sent to Siberia for maintaining Jewish religious life. After international intervention secured his release, he settled in London and became Av Beit Din of the London Beth Din, shaping British Orthodoxy for decades. Later he moved to Jerusalem, where he taught Torah until his passing. He is best known as the author of the monumental Tosefta commentary 'Chazon Yechezkel'.

name: Rabbi Isser Yehuda Unterman
bio: Third Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel (1964–1972), previously Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv and Liverpool. A Mizrachi leader, renowned halachic authority, and disciple of Rabbi Shimon Shkop, he combined traditional Litvak methodology with attention to modern halachic issues.

name: Rabbi Yosef Shlomo Kahaneman
bio: Orthodox rabbi, rosh yeshiva of Ponevezh, founder of the re-established Ponevezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak, member of Agudath Israel’s Council of Torah Sages.

name: ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יצחק זאב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (19 October 1886–11 October 1959), known as the Griz or Brisker Rav, was the last rabbi of prewar Brisk and a central transmitter of the Brisker analytical method. He was born in Volozhin while his father ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק taught there; his mother Lifsha was a daughter of ר׳ רפאל שפירא. After the family moved to Brisk, his father became his principal teacher. He married Alte Hendel Auerbach and succeeded ר׳ חיים as rabbi of Brisk after the latter's death in 1918. His learning emphasized exact textual formulation, conceptual distinctions within halakhic categories and especially close analysis of Rambam's משנה תורה. He also supervised the difficult publication of his father's חידושי רבנו חיים הלוי in 1936. The German invasion of Poland found him away from Brisk at Krynica. He reached Warsaw and then Vilna, escaping to Mandatory Palestine with several children in 1941; his wife and children who remained behind were murdered in the Holocaust. In Jerusalem he declined formal state or chief-rabbinic office and taught a small selected circle in his home, from which the later Jerusalem Brisk yeshivot developed under his sons. He became an influential leader of anti-Zionist Lithuanian Haredi society, opposing participation in state institutions and policies he believed threatened religious autonomy. His own writings were published principally after his death as חידושי מרן רי״ז הלוי on Rambam, Torah and Talmudic tractates; student notebooks form a related but textually distinct literature. He died in Jerusalem in 1959 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
base_name: Yitzchak Zev HaLevi Soloveitchik, the Brisker Rav
title: הגרי״ז — הרב מבריסק

name: Joel Teitelbaum
bio: Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum (1887–1979) was the founding Rebbe of the Satmar Hasidic dynasty and a leading post-Holocaust Hasidic figure. Born in Sighet, Hungary, the youngest son of Rabbi Chananyah Yom Tov Lipa Teitelbaum, he became known for his deep scholarship, charisma, and fierce opposition to Zionism. After surviving the Holocaust via the Kastner train, he rebuilt Satmar in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, where his followers established Congregation Yetev Lev. He later became President of the Edah HaChareidis in Jerusalem and authored the sefer 'Vayoel Moshe,' articulating his anti-Zionist ideology. Under his leadership, Satmar grew into the largest Hasidic movement in the world. His legacy includes Kiryas Joel, a Hasidic enclave named in his honor, and a vast network of institutions worldwide.
title: Satmar Rebbe, founder of the Satmar Hasidic dynasty

name: יצחק הלוי הרצוג (Yitzchak HaLevi Herzog)
bio: Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi Herzog (1888–1959) was the first Chief Rabbi of the State of Israel and previously Chief Rabbi of Ireland. Known as the 'Sinai of his generation' for his vast Torah knowledge, he worked tirelessly to integrate Jewish law into the emerging State of Israel, while also striving to rescue European Jewry during and after the Holocaust. He was the father of Israeli President Chaim Herzog and grandfather of current President Isaac Herzog.

name: ישראל אבוחצירא (Baba Sali)
bio: Rabbi Yisrael Abuhatzeira (1889–1984), known as the Baba Sali, was a revered Moroccan-Israeli kabbalist and tzaddik. Famous for his piety, blessings, and miracles, he became a spiritual leader for Moroccan Jewry and later for Jews throughout Israel. His yahrzeit is widely commemorated with mass pilgrimages to his tomb in Netivot.

name: Kalonymus Kalman Szapiro
bio: Rabbi Kalonymus Kalman Szapiro (1889–1943), known as the Piaseczner Rebbe, was a Hasidic leader, educator, and one of the most profound spiritual voices of the Holocaust. A grandson of the Maor VaShemesh, he became rabbi of Piaseczno near Warsaw and founded the yeshiva Da’as Moshe. His works, including Chovas HaTalmidim and Bnei Machshava Tova, reshaped Hasidic education for modern youth. Confined in the Warsaw Ghetto during World War II, he sustained his followers with clandestine Torah discourses later published as 'Esh Kodesh,' a unique testimony of faith under persecution. He was murdered in Trawniki during Aktion Erntefest in 1943, and posthumously recognized as a spiritual guide for generations.
title: Piaseczner Rebbe, author of Esh Kodesh

name: ר׳ ראובן מרגליות
bio: ר׳ ראובן מרגליות (30 November 1889–28 August 1971), commonly rendered Reuben or Reuven Margolies, was a Galician-born Israeli rabbinic scholar, editor, bibliographer and librarian. Born in Lemberg to Moshe and Miriam Margolies, he studied with ר׳ משה זאב מזוזה and ר׳ דוד טוניס but developed chiefly through intensive independent study. After his father's death he managed the family business and later operated a Hebrew bookshop that became a meeting place for scholars. He received rabbinic ordination in 1914 from ר׳ מאיר אריק and ר׳ משה באב״ד, yet declined a salaried rabbinate. During the First World War he fled to Vienna and hid from Austro-Hungarian conscription while composing נפש חיה. In Galicia he published prolifically and held posts in Mizrachi and Zionist institutions. Following the death of his first wife, Chaya Gendil, he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1934 and settled in Tel Aviv. From then until retirement in 1967 he directed the Rambam Library, developing it from a tiny collection into a major rabbinic research library. His more than fifty books joined traditional erudition with bibliography, textual comparison, biography, halakhah, Talmud and Kabbalah. Especially influential were מרגליות הים on Sanhedrin, יסוד המשנה ועריכתה, editions of ספר חסידים and responsa מן השמים, and his annotated editions of the Zoharic corpus. He disputed גרשם שלום's interpretation of the ר׳ יעקב עמדין–ר׳ יהונתן אייבשיץ controversy. Awarded the Israel Prize for rabbinic literature in 1957, he died at Ichilov Hospital and was buried in Nahalat Yitzhak Cemetery.
title: חוקר תורני, מהדיר וספרן

name: ר׳ אברהם חיים נאה (Avraham Chaim Naeh)
bio: Rav Avraham Chaim Naeh (1890–1954) was a leading posek in Jerusalem, renowned for establishing standard halachic measurements (shiurim). Born in Hebron, he studied in Jerusalem under the leading rabbis of the Old Yishuv and later became dayan and halachic authority of the Chabad community. His works Kezot HaShulchan and Shiurei Torah became foundational in clarifying halachic practice.

name: יעקב קמינצקי (Yaakov Kamenetsky)
bio: Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky (1891–1986) was a Lithuanian-American Torah scholar and Rosh Yeshiva of Torah Vodaath in Brooklyn. A student of Slabodka and a close colleague of Rav Aharon Kotler, he became a leading figure in American Orthodoxy. Known for his clarity, humility, and warmth, he authored Emes L’Yaakov on Torah and halacha, and played a central role in building Torah life in the United States.

name: Zvi Yehudah Kook
bio: Rosh Yeshiva of Mercaz HaRav, leader in Religious Zionism.

name: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר
bio: ר׳ אהרן קוטלר (1892–1962), born Aharon Pines in Svislach, was a Lithuanian-trained rosh yeshiva who became a principal architect of postwar American yeshiva life. Orphaned young, he studied in Krynki and Minsk before entering Yeshivat Knesset Yisrael in Slabodka, where ר׳ נתן צבי פינקל and ר׳ משה מרדכי אפשטיין shaped his learning. After marrying Chana Perel, daughter of ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר, he taught in Slutsk and from 1917 served as a regular maggid shiur. Communist pressure led him and many students across the border to Kletsk in 1921; there he built a major Polish-Lithuanian yeshiva and helped organize Vaad Hayeshivot. After Germany invaded Poland, the yeshiva regrouped in Vilna and then Jonava. Soviet authorities closed it in early 1941, and ר׳ אהרן escaped through Siberia and Japan to the United States. He immediately joined Vaad Hatzalah's efforts to rescue rabbis and yeshiva students trapped in Europe. In 1943 he founded Beth Medrash Govoha in Lakewood, deliberately locating intensive full-time Torah study away from New York's distractions. From a small opening group it became the institutional model for a large American kollel and yeshiva culture. He also led Agudath Israel of America's Council of Torah Sages, supported Torah Umesorah and helped establish and sustain Chinuch Atzmai in Israel. His surviving teachings—largely edited after his death as משנת רבי אהרן—combine close Talmudic analysis, lectures on Jewish thought, responsa and institutional correspondence. He died at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center in New York on 29 November 1962 and was buried on Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.
title: ראש ישיבת בית מדרש גבוה וממנהיגי עולם הישיבות בארצות הברית
aliases: רבי אהרן בן שניאור זלמן קוטלר

name: אליהו אליעזר דסלר (Eliyahu Eliezer Dessler)
bio: Rabbi Eliyahu Eliezer Dessler (1892–1953) was a rabbi, mussar teacher, and thinker, best known for his collected teachings published as 'Michtav Me’Eliyahu'. A student of the Kelm Talmud Torah, he became mashgiach in Gateshead (England) and later at the Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. His writings emphasize free will, spiritual growth, and the struggle between giving and taking.

name: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין
bio: ר׳ משה פיינשטיין (3 March 1895–23 March 1986) was a Belarusian-born American rosh yeshivah and halakhic decisor whose responsa became central to twentieth-century Orthodox practice. Born in Uzda to ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין and Faya Gittel, he learned first from his father and later in Slutsk and Shklov, regarding ר׳ פסח פרוסקין as his principal teacher; ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר and his uncle ר׳ יעקב קנטרוביץ were also formative influences. He married Shima Kustanovich in 1920. From 1921 until leaving the Soviet Union he served as rabbi of Lyuban, sustaining communal religious life under increasing state pressure. The family reached New York in January 1937 and settled on the Lower East Side. At Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem he developed its advanced beit midrash and semikhah programme and, after 1938, served as rosh yeshivah. Rabbis and individuals worldwide submitted practical questions to him concerning ritual, family law, commerce, medicine, technology and American communal life. His method combined close Talmudic analysis with direct attention to facts and human circumstances, though particular rulings sometimes drew disagreement from other Orthodox authorities. Seven volumes of אגרות משה appeared during his lifetime and additional material was edited posthumously. His תלמוד commentary דברות משה and Torah discourses דרש משה represent other parts of his scholarship. He chaired Agudath Israel of America's Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah, led the Union of Orthodox Rabbis and advised Torah Umesorah and Chinuch Atzmai. He died in New York and was buried at Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.
title: פוסק וראש מתיבתא תפארת ירושלים

name: Sir Israel Brodie
bio: Chief Rabbi of Great Britain and the Commonwealth (1948–1965). A dignified leader, mellifluous preacher, and organiser of the Conference of European Rabbis, he helped rebuild European Jewry after the Holocaust and oversaw the post-war expansion of Anglo-Jewry. He was the first Chief Rabbi to be knighted.

name: Elazar Menachem Man Shach
bio: Haredi rabbi, Gadol HaDor of Lithuanian Jewry in Israel, rosh yeshiva at Ponevezh Yeshiva, political leader, and founder of Degel HaTorah.

name: ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי
bio: ר׳ יעקב ישראל קניבסקי (17 June 1899–10 August 1985), commonly called the Steipler and בעל קהלות יעקב, was a Novardok-trained Talmudist, yeshiva teacher, author, and influential leader of Lithuanian Haredi Judaism in Israel. He was born in Tashan, Ukraine, to ר׳ חיים פרץ קניבסקי and Bracha; after his father’s death the family returned to Hornostaypil, the town from which his enduring sobriquet was derived. He entered the Novardok yeshiva network as a boy, followed it east to Homel during the First World War, endured conscription into the Red Army, and later crossed into Poland to join its Białystok centre. In 1927 he married Pesha Miriam Karelitz, sister of ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ, and served as a senior lecturer at Beit Yosef–Novardok in Pinsk. In 1934 he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine and became head of the movement’s Beit Yosef yeshiva in Bnei Brak. His analytical studies, first issued in separate volumes and later reorganized as קהלות יעקב on the Talmud, became his principal scholarly legacy. He also wrote on biblical interpretation, faith, ethics, Torah study, and halakhic measurements; his correspondence was collected posthumously. Although increasingly consulted for counsel and communal guidance, he devoted most of his time to study, writing, teaching, and receiving petitioners. He died in Bnei Brak and was buried beside ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ in the Shomrei Shabbos cemetery.
title: הסטייפלר; בעל קהלות יעקב

name: ר׳ חיים לייב הלוי שמואלביץ
bio: ר׳ חיים לייב הלוי שמואלביץ (1902–1979) was a leading Lithuanian Talmudist, mussar teacher and rosh yeshiva of Mir. Born in Kovno and raised partly in Stutchin, he studied at Shaarei Torah in Grodno under ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ before joining Mir about 1924–25. He married Chana Miriam, daughter of ר׳ אליעזר יהודה פינקל, and began giving regular shiurim in 1936. During the Second World War he helped lead Mir's extraordinary flight from Soviet-occupied Lithuania through Vladivostok and Kobe to Shanghai. With ר׳ יחזקאל לוינשטיין he sustained the refugee yeshiva's learning and communal life there until 1947. After six months with the transplanted yeshiva in the United States, he joined Mir in Jerusalem, becoming its rosh yeshiva after his father-in-law's death in 1965. His analytical Talmud lectures reflected the influence of ר׳ שמעון יהודה שקופ, while his intensely delivered ethical discourses drew large audiences. שיחות מוסר, based on talks delivered in 1971–73, became an influential mussar classic; extensive Talmudic manuscripts were published posthumously as שערי חיים. He died in Jerusalem on 3 Tevet 5739 and was buried at Har HaMenuchot.
title: ראש ישיבת מיר בליטא, בשנחאי ובירושלים

name: ר׳ מנחם מענדל שניאורסון
bio: ר׳ מנחם מענדל שניאורסון (18 April 1902–12 June 1994), the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, transformed Chabad-Lubavitch from a displaced Hasidic court into an international network of religious education, outreach and social institutions. Born in Nikolaev, he grew up in Yekaterinoslav, where his father ר׳ לוי יצחק שניאורסון served as rabbi and kabbalist under the Russian Empire and Soviet rule. He married Chaya Mushka, daughter of ר׳ יוסף יצחק שניאורסון, in Warsaw in 1928. The couple lived in Berlin and Paris; he studied university subjects in Berlin and earned an engineering diploma in Paris in 1937, while continuing Torah study and work for his father-in-law. They escaped occupied France and reached New York in 1941. He directed Merkos L’Inyonei Chinuch, Machne Israel and Kehot before accepting Chabad leadership in 1951. From 770 Eastern Parkway he expanded shlichut, sending couples to build enduring Jewish institutions, and promoted public mitzvah campaigns, Torah publication, women’s education and use of modern communications for religious purposes. His talks and letters address halakhah, Hasidic thought, biblical interpretation, science, education and public affairs. In his final years, messianic expectation intensified among followers; after his death without a successor, interpretations of those expectations remained contested within Chabad. His institutional system nevertheless continued expanding globally.
title: הרבי מליובאוויטש השביעי

name: ר׳ יהושע דוד פוברסקי
bio: ר׳ יהושע דוד פוברסקי (1902–1999), generally called ר׳ דוד פוברסקי, was a Lithuanian-style Talmudist, mussar teacher and rosh yeshiva who shaped more than five decades of learning at the rebuilt Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. Born David Kustonowitz in Lyuban to ר׳ שלום, he studied as a boy in Slutsk with ר׳ איסר זלמן מלצר. During the First World War he crossed wartime borders using papers bearing the name Yehoshua Povarsky; he retained that surname and added Yehoshua to his own name. His formative education passed through the displaced Slabodka and Mir yeshivot, the Kelm Talmud Torah and the prewar Ponovezh world. ר׳ ירוחם ליבוביץ profoundly influenced his mussar outlook. After marrying Tzipporah, daughter of ר׳ דוד דב קרייזר, he studied in the Baranovich circle of ר׳ אלחנן וסרמן and also delivered shiurim. He escaped Europe with his family in 1941 and initially headed the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Tel Aviv. In 1944 ר׳ יוסף שלמה כהנמן recruited him to lead the newly re-established Ponovezh Yeshiva beside ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי; ר׳ אלעזר מנחם מן שך later joined its senior leadership. His teaching combined exact textual analysis, conceptual clarity, the disciplined ethical inheritance of Kelm and close personal responsibility for students. He avoided political prominence and centered his public life on daily learning and transmission. His Talmudic novellae and lectures were published in the multi-volume ישועת דוד and שיעורי ר׳ דוד, while ישמרו דעת and משכיל לדוד preserve his mussar discourses.
title: ראש ישיבת פוניבז׳ ובעל ישועת דוד

name: ר׳ יצחק יעקב וייס
bio: ר׳ יצחק יעקב וייס (15 February 1902–14 June 1989), known from his responsa as the מנחת יצחק, was a Galician-born halakhic decisor and rabbinical judge. Born in Dolyna, he moved with his family during the First World War to Munkács, where he studied under his father ר׳ יוסף יהודה וייס and received ordination from ר׳ חיים אלעזר שפירא; ר׳ מאיר אריק and ר׳ שמעון גרינפלד further shaped his practical-halakhic method. After marrying the daughter of ר׳ פנחס צימטבוים, he became a dayan in Grosswardein (Oradea) in 1929. He survived the Holocaust through hiding and a perilous escape into Romania, but his first wife died in Bucharest. Returning to Oradea, he helped rebuild communal life and adjudicated difficult agunah cases. Manchester appointed him senior dayan in December 1948; for two decades he led its beth din, strengthened kashrut supervision and helped establish a rabbinic kollel. In 1970 he joined the Edah HaChareidis court in Jerusalem, became presiding raavad in 1972 and gaavad in 1979. His ten-volume שו״ת מנחת יצחק applied classical halakhah to postwar, medical, technological, commercial and ritual questions. He died in Jerusalem and was buried on the Mount of Olives.
title: בעל מנחת יצחק וגאב״ד העדה החרדית

name: ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק
bio: ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק (27 February 1903–9 April 1993), commonly called Joseph B. Soloveitchik, “the Rav,” or הגרי״ד, was a Talmudist, halakhic authority, religious philosopher and formative leader of American Modern Orthodoxy. Born in Pruzhany in the Russian Empire, he was taught the Brisker method by his father ר׳ משה סולובייצ׳יק and descended from ר׳ חיים הלוי סולובייצ׳יק and the בית הלוי. After study in Warsaw and Berlin, he completed a doctorate on Hermann Cohen and married Tonya Lewit. In 1932 they settled in Boston, where he led the Orthodox Vaad HaIr, opened a yeshivah and co-founded Maimonides School. From 1941 he succeeded his father at Yeshiva University’s Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary, commuting from Boston and ordaining close to two thousand rabbis. He led the Rabbinical Council of America’s Halakhah Commission and became an influential Religious Zionist voice. His writings joined rigorous halakhic categories with modern philosophy and existential reflection. איש ההלכה, ובקשתם משם, קול דודי דופק, “The Lonely Man of Faith,” “Confrontation” and The Halakhic Mind address religious personality, covenant, suffering, Zionism, interfaith boundaries and the relation between revelation and modern thought. He retired from regular teaching as illness advanced in the mid-1980s, died in Boston and was buried in West Roxbury.
title: הגרי״ד, ראש ישיבת רבנו יצחק אלחנן וממנהיגי האורתודוקסיה המודרנית

name: יצחק הוטנר (Yitzchak Hutner)
bio: Rabbi Yitzchak Hutner (1906–1980) was a major 20th-century Torah thinker, rosh yeshiva of Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Berlin in Brooklyn, and author of 'Pachad Yitzchak'. He combined Lithuanian Torah learning with deep philosophical and mussar insights, shaping generations of American Orthodox rabbinic leadership.

name: Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv
bio: Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv (1910–2012) was one of the foremost poskim (halakhic authorities) of the 20th–21st centuries. Born in Šiauliai, Lithuania, he moved as a child to Jerusalem, where he became a leading disciple of the Chazon Ish and developed into the undisputed halakhic leader of the Lithuanian Torah world. He served briefly as a dayan in the Rabbinical Courts before devoting himself entirely to Torah study and psak halakha. His small study hall in Mea Shearim became the center of global halakhic guidance until his passing at age 102.

name: ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך (Shlomo Zalman Auerbach)
bio: Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (1910–1995) was one of the foremost halachic authorities of the 20th century. Rosh Yeshiva of Kol Torah in Jerusalem, he was widely respected for his balanced rulings, kindness, and clarity in applying halacha to modern issues such as electricity, medicine, and technology.

name: ר׳ שמואל הלוי ואזנר
bio: ר׳ שמואל הלוי ואזנר (4 September 1913–3 April 2015), widely known as the שבט הלוי, was a Vienna-born rabbinic judge, yeshiva head and influential halakhic decisor. The son of Yosef Zvi and Rachel Wosner, he studied in Vienna and then at Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin under ר׳ מאיר שפירא and ר׳ שמעון מזליחוב. After marrying Rivka Gelber and spending time in Pressburg, he immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1939. In Jerusalem he studied at Yeshivat Dushinsky, served as a religious judge and taught in the Geula neighbourhood. At the encouragement of ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ and other senior rabbis, he moved to Bnei Brak around 1947. There he became rabbi and av beth din of the Zikhron Meir neighbourhood and re-established Yeshivat Chachmei Lublin, which he led for more than six decades. He later created a beth hora'ah and a network of communities associated with his rulings. His eleven-volume שו״ת שבט הלוי treats all divisions of the Shulchan Arukh and applies halakhah to medicine, electricity, electronic sensors, transport, kashrut and changing domestic technology. Students also published his Talmudic lectures, discourses and practical rulings. He died in Bnei Brak on the first night of Passover 2015.
title: בעל שבט הלוי ורב זכרון מאיר

name: ר׳ אהרן יהודה לייב שטיינמן (Aharon Yehuda Leib Shteinman)
bio: Rabbi Aharon Yehuda Leib Shteinman (1914–2017) was a leading Lithuanian Torah sage, Rosh Yeshiva, and spiritual guide of the Haredi world. Known for his humility, simplicity, and clarity, he served as Rosh Yeshiva of Gaon Yaakov in Bnei Brak and was widely regarded as the successor to Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv as leader of the Torah world.

name: ר׳ שלמה וולבה (Shlomo Wolbe)
bio: Rav Shlomo Wolbe (1914–2005) was a leading mussar thinker and educator in the 20th century. Born in Berlin, he studied at the Hildesheimer Rabbinical Seminary and later in Mir Yeshiva in Latvia. After surviving World War II in Sweden, he moved to Israel, where he became mashgiach of Be’er Yaakov and later founded Yeshivat Givat Shaul. He is renowned for his work Alei Shur and for shaping post-war mussar thought.

name: ר׳ אליעזר יהודה וולְדֶנברג (Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg)
bio: Rabbi Eliezer Yehuda Waldenberg (1915–2006), known as the Tzitz Eliezer, was one of the leading halachic authorities of the 20th century. A dayan on the Supreme Rabbinical Court in Jerusalem, he became renowned for his vast responsa covering Jewish law and modern medical ethics, including organ transplantation, abortion, autopsies, and end-of-life issues. His works bridged traditional halacha with contemporary challenges.

name: שלמה גורן (Shlomo Goren)
bio: Rabbi Shlomo Goren (1917–1994) was the first Chief Rabbi of the Israel Defense Forces and later Chief Rabbi of Israel. A brilliant talmid chacham and halachic authority, he became a symbol of religious Zionism and the integration of Torah with the modern Jewish state. He is remembered for blowing the shofar at the Western Wall during the Six-Day War (1967) and for his halachic rulings on issues of war, conversion, and national security.

name: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef
bio: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef (1920–2013) was the Sephardic Chief Rabbi of Israel, halakhic authority, and spiritual leader of the Shas political party. Born in Baghdad, he immigrated to Jerusalem as a child. A brilliant talmid chacham, he became Chief Rabbi of Tel Aviv and later Rishon LeZion (Sephardic Chief Rabbi of Israel, 1973–1983). His halakhic rulings, especially codified in his magnum opus Yabia Omer, revolutionized Sephardic halakha and restored pride to Sephardic Jewry. He was one of the most influential rabbis of the 20th century.

name: Immanuel Jakobovits
bio: Immanuel Jakobovits, Baron Jakobovits (1921–1999), was Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth (1967–1991). Previously Chief Rabbi of Ireland and rabbi of the Fifth Avenue Synagogue in New York, he became the first Chief Rabbi to sit in the House of Lords. He was a pioneer in Jewish medical ethics, a conservative public voice in Britain, and close to Margaret Thatcher.

name: ר׳ מרדכי ברויאר
bio: ר׳ מרדכי ברויאר (14 May 1921–24 February 2007; Marcus Breuer) was a German-born Israeli rabbi, Bible teacher and scholar of the Masoretic text. Born in Karlsruhe to ר׳ שמשון ברויאר and Leah Frankel, he was a great-grandson of ר׳ שמשון רפאל הירש. His family immigrated to Mandatory Palestine when he was twelve. He studied in Jerusalem at Horev, Yeshivat Kol Torah and Yeshivat Hebron, then taught Tanakh from 1947 in religious-Zionist schools and yeshivot, including Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh, Yeshivat HaDarom, Jerusalem College for Women and Yeshivat Har Etzion. His textual work sought the authoritative Tiberian Masoretic text by comparing manuscripts, Masorah and early printed editions. When he gained access to the Aleppo Codex, its readings closely confirmed the text he had independently reconstructed. His editions entered the Da'at Mikra series, the Horev Tanakh and, with graphic design inspired by the Aleppo Codex, כתר ירושלים—the Hebrew University's official Bible edition and the edition used for ceremonial presentations by the Knesset. Breuer also developed שיטת הבחינות, accepting many literary divisions identified by documentary criticism while interpreting the Torah's contrasting voices as intentionally revealed divine perspectives whose combination expresses a fuller truth. The method generated lasting debate within religious Bible study. His books include פיסוק טעמים שבמקרא, כתר ארם צובה והנוסח המקובל של המקרא, פרקי מועדות and פרקי בראשית. He received the Bialik Prize in 1984, the Israel Prize for original rabbinic literature in 1999, and an honorary doctorate from the Hebrew University.
title: חוקר נוסח המקרא ומפתח שיטת הבחינות

name: ר׳ חיים פרידלנדר
bio: ר׳ חיים בן משה פרידלנדר (23 June 1923–4 August 1986), known through the posthumous שפתי חיים series, was a German-born Israeli mussar teacher, educator and editor. Born in Breslau, he immigrated with his parents משה and צפורה to Mandatory Palestine shortly before the Second World War. After living at Kibbutz Hafetz Haim, he studied at the Lomza yeshivah in Petah Tikva and became one of the first seven students of the newly established Ponovezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak. There he studied closely with ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי and became a principal disciple of the mashgiach ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר. Together with ר׳ אריה כרמל he helped edit מכתב מאליהו from ר׳ דסלר's writings. He founded and directed the Torat Emet school in Bnei Brak, served as mashgiach at Yeshivat HaNegev in Netivot, and returned in 1981 as mashgiach of Ponovezh. He also prepared annotated editions of writings by ר׳ משה חיים לוצאטו. After his death, his family edited his lectures and notes as שפתי חיים and מסילות חיים בחינוך.
title: השפתי חיים

name: ר׳ גרשון אדלשטיין (Gershon Edelstein)
bio: Rabbi Gershon Edelstein (1923–2023) was Rosh Yeshiva of the Ponevezh Yeshiva in Bnei Brak and a leading authority of the Lithuanian Torah world. Known for his gentleness, clarity, and humility, he guided thousands of talmidim and, in his later years, served as the acknowledged leader of the Haredi world.

name: Rabbi Yehuda Amital
bio: Orthodox rabbi, Holocaust survivor, founder and Rosh Yeshiva of Yeshivat Har Etzion for 40 years, creator of the Hesder Yeshiva model combining Torah study with IDF service, and political leader associated with the Israeli Left. He also served briefly as a minister in the Israeli government after the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.

name: משה שטרנבוך (Moshe Sternbuch)
bio: Rabbi Moshe Sternbuch (b. 1926) is a leading halakhic authority, dayan, and rosh av beis din of the Edah HaChareidis in Jerusalem. Born in London, he studied under Rav Elchonon Wasserman and became known for his brilliance from a young age. He later served as a rabbinic leader in South Africa before settling in Israel, where he became a major posek and dayan. He is the author of Teshuvos v’Hanhagos, a widely used multi-volume responsa work.

name: R'Chaim Kanievsky
bio: Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky (1928–2022) was widely revered as the Gadol HaDor, the preeminent Litvak Torah authority of his generation. Born in Pinsk to Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael Kanievsky (the Steipler) and Pesha Miriam (sister of the Chazon Ish), he grew up in Bnei Brak, where he lived his entire adult life. Renowned for his encyclopedic mastery of Torah, he completed Shas at age 17 and later authored dozens of seforim. Thousands flocked daily to his modest home for blessings and halachic guidance. After the passing of Rav Elyashiv and Rav Shteinman, he was regarded as the supreme halachic leader of the Haredi world. His funeral in 2022 drew over half a million people, among the largest in Israel’s history.
title: Rav Chaim Kanievsky, Gadol HaDor

name: ישראל יעקב פישר (Yisrael Yaakov Fisher)
bio: Rabbi Yisrael Yaakov Fisher (1928–2003) was a leading halachic authority in Jerusalem and one of the senior dayanim of the Edah HaChareidis. He was known for his deep halachic rulings, humility, and leadership within the ultra-Orthodox community of Jerusalem.

name: נחום אליעזר רבינוביץ (Nachum Eliezer Rabinovitch)
bio: Rabbi Nachum Eliezer Rabinovitch (1928–2020) was a prominent Religious Zionist rosh yeshiva, halachic decisor, and philosopher. He served as Rosh Yeshiva of Birkat Moshe in Ma'ale Adumim for nearly four decades, authored the monumental Yad Peshutah commentary on the Rambam, and was widely respected for his clarity, intellectual honesty, and integration of Torah with science and rational philosophy.

name: ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין
bio: ר׳ דוד פיינשטיין (1929–6 November 2020) was an American rosh yeshivah, halakhic authority, communal leader and author. He was born in Lyuban, then in the Soviet Union and now in Belarus, to ר׳ משה פיינשטיין and Shima Kustanovich Feinstein. His father served as Lyuban's rabbi while maintaining religious life under increasingly hostile Soviet conditions. In January 1937 the family emigrated to New York and settled on Manhattan's Lower East Side, where ר׳ משה became head of Mesivtha Tifereth Jerusalem (MTJ). ר׳ דוד learned at MTJ under his father, later taught advanced classes there and became closely identified with both the yeshivah and the neighborhood in which he lived for the rest of his life. After his father's death in 1986, he succeeded him as rosh yeshivah of MTJ's elementary school, high school and kollel. He also became one of the most frequently consulted Orthodox decisors in the United States. The Orthodox Union sought his rulings on kashrut, youth work and new practical questions; rabbis and individuals approached him on ritual, commercial, medical and communal law. He served for decades on the Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah of Agudath Israel of America, belonged to Torah Umesorah's Vaad Roshei Yeshiva, and was involved with Chinuch Atzmai, Agudas Harabbonim and other institutions. His leadership was notable for reserve, accessibility and reluctance to cultivate public ceremony. His published Torah teaching appeared chiefly under the title קול דודי. English volumes adapted from his lectures cover the Torah, Haftarot, Esther and Ruth; other books address the Passover Seder and the structure and laws of the Jewish calendar. He also wrote the explanations of the Masoretic notes printed at the end of each weekly portion in ArtScroll's Stone Chumash. The publications often relied on compilers and adapters, so their bibliographic descriptions distinguish his authorship and lectures from editorial work by others. ר׳ דוד died in New York on 6 November 2020. After a funeral outside MTJ at 145 East Broadway, his coffin was flown to Israel; a second funeral left Jerusalem's Shamgar Funeral Home, and he was buried on Har HaMenuchot near ר׳ משה פיינשטיין. His significance lies in the combination of institutional continuity, practical halakhic judgment, wide communal responsibility and a deliberately understated personal manner.
title: ראש ישיבת מתיבתא תפארת ירושלים ופוסק הלכה

name: ר׳ אברהם יהושע העשיל טברסקי
bio: ר׳ אברהם יהושע העשיל טברסקי (6 October 1930–31 January 2021), commonly known as Rabbi Dr. Abraham J. Twerski, was an American Hasidic rabbi, psychiatrist, addiction specialist and prolific author. Born in Milwaukee, he was a son of ר׳ יעקב ישראל טברסקי of Hornosteipel and Devorah Leah Halberstam, linking the Chernobyl and Bobov dynasties. He graduated from Hebrew Theological College and received semikhah in 1951, then served beside his father at Congregation Beth Jehudah. Concluding that effective pastoral counseling required professional training, he entered Marquette University and completed medical school in 1960. He moved to Pittsburgh, where he became clinical director of psychiatry at St. Francis Hospital and an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. In 1972 he opened Gateway Rehabilitation Center in Beaver County, developing a treatment model that joined medicine, Twelve-Step recovery, spirituality and restoration of self-worth. He later helped establish Shaar Hatikvah for released prisoners in Israel. Across more than sixty books—clinical, self-help, Jewish ethical, autobiographical and Torah works—he repeatedly addressed addiction, shame, self-esteem, family relationships, domestic abuse and spiritual growth. He moved to Jerusalem in 2015 and died there from complications of COVID-19. His work made addiction treatment and previously hidden family problems subjects of sustained discussion within Orthodox Jewish communities.
title: רב חסידי, פסיכיאטר ומחלוצי הטיפול בהתמכרויות

name: ר׳ אפרים דב לנדו
bio: ר׳ אפרים דב לנדו (born 5 April 1930), generally known as ר׳ דב לנדו or Rav Dov Lando, is an Israeli rosh yeshiva and leader of the Lithuanian-Haredi community. He was born in Zgierz near Łódź, Poland, to ר׳ טוביה יוסף לנדוי and Devorah, in a family descended from the Strikov Hasidic dynasty. The family immigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1935 and settled in Rehovot. After studying at Yeshivat HaYishuv HeHadash, he entered Ponovezh Yeshiva, where his principal teachers included ר׳ דוד פוברסקי and ר׳ שמואל רוזובסקי; he also learned for a period with ר׳ אליהו אליעזר דסלר. He subsequently spent about a year at Hebron Yeshiva and regarded ר׳ אברהם ישעיהו קרליץ as his formative halakhic and intellectual authority. He married Adina, a descendant of the Slabodka leadership, and joined Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak as a teacher. In the early 1980s he became one of its roshei yeshiva, eventually serving alongside ר׳ משה הלל הירש. His published scholarship includes זכר טוב, זכר דבר, מנחת דבר, חידושי רבי דב לנדו, גליונות רבי דב לנדו and the correspondence שיח דבר. Since 2023 he has held a central public-leadership role and serves as president of Vaad HaYeshivot.
title: ראש ישיבת סלבודקה ונשיא ועד הישיבות

name: Dayan Chanoch Ehrentreu
bio: German-born British Orthodox rabbi. He served as head (Rosh) of the London Beth Din (1984–2006), where he was a leading halachic authority, especially in medical ethics, conversions, and kashrut. He established the Sunderland Kollel, served as Av Beth Din in Manchester, and later guided the creation of the North-West London eruv.

name: ר׳ משה הלל הירש (Moshe Hillel Hirsch)
bio: Rabbi Moshe Hillel Hirsch (b. 1932) is the Rosh Yeshiva of Slabodka Yeshiva in Bnei Brak and a member of the Moetzes Gedolei HaTorah. A talmid of the Chevron Yeshiva and close disciple of Rav Aharon Kotler, he is known for his penetrating shiurim and guidance to talmidim.

name: Rabbi Aharon Lichtenstein
bio: Orthodox rabbi, rosh yeshiva, and Israel Prize laureate. Born in Paris, raised in the U.S., he studied under Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik (his future father-in-law) and earned a PhD in English Literature from Harvard. He served as Rosh Kollel at Yeshiva University before making aliyah to join Rabbi Yehuda Amital at Yeshivat Har Etzion in 1971. Known for integrating rigorous Torah study with a centrist Orthodox embrace of modernity, he became one of the most influential Torah leaders of his generation.

name: אריה קפלן (Aryeh Kaplan)
bio: Rabbi Aryeh Kaplan (1934–1983) was an American Orthodox rabbi, physicist, and prolific author, known for making complex Jewish mystical and philosophical concepts accessible. With a background in physics and deep knowledge of Kabbalah, he wrote over 50 works during his short lifetime, including translations, commentaries, and original books. His writings continue to inspire ba'alei teshuva, scholars, and seekers worldwide.

name: R'Yitzchok Zilberstein
bio: Rabbi Yitzchok Zilberstein (b. 1934) is a prominent halachic authority, dayan, and posek in Bnei Brak. Son-in-law of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, he is known for his clarity in medical halacha and practical rulings. He serves as Rav of Ramat Elchanan in Bnei Brak.

name: ר׳ משה שפירא
bio: ר׳ משה שפירא (28 May 1935–7 January 2017), commonly rendered Rav Moshe Shapira or Shapiro, was an Israeli rosh yeshiva and one of the most influential contemporary teachers of Jewish thought and aggadah. Born in Petah Tikva to ר׳ יצחק מאיר שפירא and Rachel, he inherited the Kelm mussar tradition through his father’s family. He studied at Ohr Yisrael, Ponevezh, Knesset Yisrael–Hebron and Beit Yehuda, absorbing the approaches of ר׳ יעקב ניימן, ר׳ יוסף רוזובסקי, ר׳ יחיאל מיכל פיינשטיין and ר׳ יצחק הוטנר. He helped establish Yeshivat Tushiya at Tifrach and Yeshivat Beit HaTalmud, later led Beis Binyomin in Stamford, and taught generations of students in Jerusalem, especially at Ohr Somayach and the Wolfson kollelim. His teaching united close Talmudic analysis with Maharal, the Vilna Gaon and his school, Kabbalah, Hasidic thought and mussar. Much of his influence was oral: students recorded and edited extensive lecture series, including רעה אמונה, אפיקי מים, ממעמקים and שיעורי הגר״מ שפירא. He also guided outreach and adult-education organizations and founded institutions for advanced study. His densely structured lectures shaped a broad network of yeshiva educators and ba’alei teshuvah teachers in Israel and abroad.
title: ראש ישיבה, בעל מחשבה ומורה לאגדה

name: אביגדור נבנצאל (Avigdor Nebenzahl)
bio: Rabbi Avigdor Nebenzahl (b. 1935) is an Israeli posek and Torah scholar, serving as the Chief Rabbi of the Old City of Jerusalem. A close disciple of Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, he is known for his halachic rulings, clarity in teaching, and humility. He has authored numerous sefarim on Tanach and halacha and is considered one of the foremost living halachic authorities in Israel.

name: ר׳ סיריל קליין האריס (Cyril K. Harris)
bio: Rabbi Cyril Kitchener Harris (1936–2005) served as Chief Rabbi of South Africa from 1987 to 2004. A British-born rabbi educated at Jews’ College, London, he became known for his moral leadership during the end of apartheid. He worked closely with Nelson Mandela and emphasized reconciliation, justice, and Jewish responsibility in society.

name: ר׳ זלמן ברוך מלמד (Zalman Baruch Melamed)
bio: Rabbi Zalman Baruch Melamed (b. 20 July 1937 / 12 Av 5697) is a senior Religious Zionist rabbi, founder and Rosh Yeshiva of Yeshivat Beit El, and a leading disciple of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook. Born in Tel Aviv, he studied at Yeshivat Kfar HaRoeh, briefly at Knesset Hezekiah in Zikhron Yaakov, helped establish Yeshivat Kerem B’Yavneh, and moved in 1954 to Mercaz HaRav in Jerusalem. He became a ram there in 1965. In 1977–78, at Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook’s direction, he led students to establish a new yeshiva and community at Beit El, where he became a central rabbinic leader. He later founded Arutz Sheva and the Vaad Rabanei Yesha, developed a network of Torah institutions, and served as rabbi of Beit El until 2013. He remains Rosh Yeshiva of Beit El and an influential teacher of Torah, emunah and Religious Zionist thought.

name: ר׳ ישראל מאיר לאו
bio: ר׳ ישראל מאיר לאו (born 1937) is a Holocaust survivor, author, communal rabbi, former Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel and chairman of the Yad Vashem Council. Born in Piotrków Trybunalski to ר׳ משה חיים לאו and Chaya, he was known as Lulek. His father and much of the community were murdered at Treblinka. In 1944 his mother saved him during a selection by directing him toward his older brother Naphtali; she was murdered at Ravensbrück. The brothers endured the Częstochowa labor camp and Buchenwald, where American forces liberated the eight-year-old child in April 1945. They reached Mandatory Palestine that summer. Raised initially by his uncle ר׳ מרדכי פוגלמן in Kiryat Motzkin, he later studied at Kol Torah with ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבאך and at Knesset Hezekiah and Ponovezh. Ordained in 1960, he advanced through synagogue and neighborhood rabbinates in Tel Aviv, became chief rabbi of Netanya in 1979, chief rabbi of Tel Aviv–Jaffa in 1988, and Ashkenazi Chief Rabbi of Israel from 1993 to 2003. He returned to the Tel Aviv post from 2005 until retiring in 2018. His rabbinate emphasized public communication, Holocaust memory, interreligious dialogue and engagement across religious and secular Israeli society. Awarded the Israel Prize for lifetime achievement in 2005, he has chaired the Yad Vashem Council since 2008. His autobiography אל תשלח ידך אל הנער connects the child survivor’s memory to his later religious leadership.
title: הרב הראשי לישראל לשעבר ויו״ר מועצת יד ושם

name: ר׳ גרשון לופיאן
bio: ר׳ גרשון לופיאן (approximately 1938–30 January 2014) was a British dayan, communal rabbi and widely consulted halakhic authority. He was the eldest son of ר׳ אריה לייב לופיאן, later rosh yeshiva in Gateshead, and Tzipa, and a grandson of the mussar teacher ר׳ אליהו לופיאן. His education linked the British and Israeli yeshiva worlds: he learned at Gateshead Yeshiva, under his grandfather at Kfar Hasidim, at Hebron Yeshiva in Jerusalem, and under ר׳ חנוך העניך אהרנטרוי at Sunderland Kollel. Sources report that he received semikhah from ר׳ שלמה זלמן אויערבך, ר׳ חנוך העניך פאדווא and ר׳ משה פיינשטיין. From 1976 until retiring in 2006 he led Yeshurun Federation Synagogue in Edgware, afterward remaining its emeritus rabbi. As a dayan of the Federation of Synagogues he became especially known for practical rulings concerning family law, niddah and marital difficulties. Memorial accounts consistently emphasize that he answered questions at all hours, considered the circumstances of the individual rather than treating halakhah mechanically, and trained younger rabbis through practical shimush and semikhah. After retirement he continued making himself available by telephone for questions from Britain and abroad. He died in London on 30 January 2014 and was buried the next day at Edmonton Federation Cemetery. The Federation’s later ShailaText service was dedicated to his memory as an extension of his accessible, confidential model of pastoral halakhic guidance.
title: דיין, פוסק ורב קהילת ישורון באדג׳וור

name: ר׳ יעקב אריה אלתר
bio: ר׳ יעקב אריה אלתר (born 18 May 1939) is the eighth Gerrer Rebbe and a senior leader of Agudath Israel's rabbinic council. He was born in Łódź to ר׳ שמחה בונים אלתר, later the sixth Gerrer Rebbe and author of לב שמחה, and Yuta Hena, a daughter of ר׳ נחמיה אלתר. He was named for ר׳ יעקב אריה גוטרמן of Radzymin. In 1940, amid the destruction of Polish Jewish life, he left Europe with his father and grandfather ר׳ אברהם מרדכי אלתר and reached Mandatory Palestine. He grew up in Jerusalem, studied at the Etz Chaim Talmud Torah and was formed within the post-war rebuilding of Ger. He married Shoshana, daughter of ר׳ מנחם מנדל וייץ, a leader of Yeshivat Chiddushei HaRim. For many years he lived and studied in Bnei Brak, particularly at the Rashi Shtiebel. After his father became Rebbe in 1977, ר׳ יעקב אריה increasingly handled institutional and political affairs for Ger and Agudath Israel. His uncle ר׳ פינחס מנחם אלתר led the dynasty from 1992 until March 1996; following his death, ר׳ יעקב אריה succeeded him. His leadership has centred on an extensive network of Gerrer synagogues, yeshivot, kollelim and schools in Israel and diaspora communities, alongside membership in the presidium of מועצת גדולי התורה. He relocated from Bnei Brak to Jerusalem in 2011, and the movement's principal court and large central beit midrash are now based there. Because he is living, reports concerning wealth, politics and internal disputes are treated as contemporary claims requiring careful sourcing rather than settled biography. No independently authored major sefer is securely catalogued under his name; published institutional volumes chiefly preserve addresses, guidance or events held in his presence.
title: האדמו״ר מגור

name: Rabbi Hershel Schachter
bio: American Orthodox rabbi, posek, and rosh yeshiva at RIETS (Yeshiva University). A close student and assistant of Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik, he became the youngest rosh yeshiva at RIETS in 1967. Widely regarded as one of the leading modern Orthodox halakhic authorities, he has written responsa on medical ethics, Jewish law during the COVID-19 pandemic, conversion, and communal leadership.

name: נתן צבי פינקל (Nosson Tzvi Finkel)
bio: Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel (1943–2011) was the Rosh Yeshiva of the Mir Yeshiva in Jerusalem, one of the largest yeshivot in the world. Born in Chicago, he was a descendant of the Alter of Slabodka and came to Israel as a teenager. Despite suffering from Parkinson’s disease for decades, he built Mir into a massive Torah center with thousands of students. Known for his fiery mussar talks, personal warmth, and devotion to Torah.

name: החלבן (Rav Yaakov Moshe Hillel)
bio: Rav Yaakov Moshe Hillel (b. 1945), known as the 'Chalban' (the Milkman), is a leading contemporary kabbalist in Jerusalem. He heads Yeshivat Ahavat Shalom, has authored numerous works on Kabbalah and Jewish thought, and is renowned for his spiritual guidance. His nickname 'Chalban' came from his family’s dairy business.

name: ר׳ יונתן זקס
bio: ר׳ יונתן זקס (8 March 1948–7 November 2020), formally ר׳ יעקב צבי בן דוד אריה, was a British Orthodox rabbi, philosopher, educator, broadcaster, and public intellectual. Born in Lambeth and educated in Finchley, Cambridge, Oxford, London, and rabbinical colleges, he credited formative 1968 conversations with ר׳ יוסף דוב סולובייצ׳יק and ר׳ מנחם מנדל שניאורסון with directing him toward the rabbinate. After serving Golders Green and Western Marble Arch synagogues and leading Jews’ College, he became Chief Rabbi of the United Hebrew Congregations of the Commonwealth in 1991 and served until 2013. He promoted Jewish education, communal renewal, interfaith responsibility, and an intellectually confident Judaism able to engage modern democratic society. His writing joined Torah commentary with moral philosophy and public theology, addressing covenant, human dignity, religious violence, science, politics, and social fragmentation. He published more than forty books, delivered the annual Covenant & Conversation commentaries, and taught at institutions including King’s College London, New York University, and Yeshiva University. Knighted in 2005, he entered the House of Lords as the crossbench life peer Baron Sacks of Aldgate in 2009 and received the Templeton Prize in 2016. He died in London after cancer and was buried at Bushey New Cemetery. His speeches, manuscripts, correspondence, and Chief Rabbinate papers are preserved in the National Library of Israel.
title: Chief Rabbi; Baron Sacks of Aldgate

name: האדמו״ר מבעלז (Yissachar Dov Rokeach)
bio: Rabbi Yissachar Dov Rokeach (b. 1948) is the Belzer Rebbe, who rebuilt the Belz Chassidic dynasty after the Holocaust. Known for his organizational skill and visionary leadership, he established schools, yeshivot, and a massive Beis Medrash in Jerusalem.

name: ר' שמעון גרשון רוזנברג (Rav Shagar)
bio: Rabbi Shimon Gershon Rosenberg (1949–2007), widely known as Rav Shagar, was a leading Israeli Religious-Zionist thinker and educator. A student of Yeshivat Kerem B’Yavneh, he later co-founded Yeshivat Siach Yitzchak. Rav Shagar integrated traditional Torah study with postmodern philosophy, Hasidut, and existentialist thought, offering a unique path for contemporary Jewish spirituality.

name: אשר וייס (Asher Weiss)
bio: Rabbi Asher Weiss (b. 1953) is a leading halakhic authority, Rosh Kollel of Machon Minchas Asher in Jerusalem, and posek for Shaarei Tzedek Medical Center. He is known for his vast Torah knowledge, clarity in psak halakha, and ability to address complex issues of modern life and medicine. Author of the acclaimed 'Minchas Asher' series, he is sought worldwide for halakhic rulings.

name: האדמו״ר מויז׳ניץ (Yisroel Hager)
bio: Rabbi Yisroel Hager (b. 1954) is the Vizhnitz Rebbe in Bnei Brak, son of the Yeshuos Moshe. Known for his warmth and charisma, he leads one of the largest Chassidic communities in Israel with thousands of followers.

name: ר׳ מיכאל רוזנצוויג
bio: ר׳ מיכאל רוזנצוויג (born 22 December 1956) is a Canadian-born American rosh yeshiva, Talmudist and historian of medieval halakhah. Raised in the scholarly and communal environment of his father ר׳ ברל רוזנצוויג, he studied in Queens under ר׳ ירוחם בוברובסקי, at Yeshivat Har Etzion under ר׳ אהרן ליכטנשטיין, and at Yeshiva University for six years under ר׳ יוסף דוב הלוי סולובייצ׳יק. He graduated summa cum laude from Yeshiva College in 1980, received semikhah from the Rabbi Isaac Elchanan Theological Seminary, and continued in its Gruss Kollel Elyon. At the Bernard Revel Graduate School he earned an M.A. and a 1996 Ph.D. in medieval Jewish history under Professor ר׳ חיים סולובייצ׳יק; his dissertation studied debt collection in absentia as halakhah responded to a mobile commercial society. Appointed a RIETS rosh yeshiva in 1985, he now holds the Nathan and Perel Schupf Chair in Talmud. Since 1997 he has led the Beren Institute for Advanced Talmudic Studies, training senior scholars and future communal rabbis. His method expands conceptual Brisker analysis through systematic comparison of Rishonim, attention to legal structure and historical development, and investigation of the religious values expressed by halakhic institutions. His publications address halakhic pluralism, creativity in divine service, Talmudic methodology and repentance; his book מימיני מיכאל integrates legal analysis and Jewish thought around Yom Kippur and teshuvah. He remains an active RIETS teacher and prolific lecturer.
title: ראש ישיבה בישיבת רבינו יצחק אלחנן וראש כולל ברן עליון

name: ר׳ אשר אריאלי (Asher Arieli)
bio: Rabbi Asher Arieli (b. 1957) is the senior maggid shiur of the Mir Yeshiva in Jerusalem. His daily shiur, attended by over a thousand students, is considered one of the largest regular Torah lectures in the world. He is renowned for his clarity, depth, and ability to connect intricate Talmudic sugyot across the Bavli and Rishonim.

name: ר' אליעזר מלמד
bio: Rabbi Eliezer Melamed (born 28 June 1961 / 14 Tammuz 5721) is an Israeli Religious Zionist rabbi, halakhic author and educator. Born in Jerusalem to Rabbi Zalman Baruch Melamed and Shulamit Melamed, he studied at Yeshivat Horev, Yeshivat Yerushalayim LeTzeirim and for approximately six years at Yeshivat Mercaz HaRav. Among his principal teachers were Rabbi Zvi Yehuda HaKohen Kook and Rabbi Avraham Shapira. He received rabbinic ordination in 1988. In August 1988 he became rabbi of Har Bracha, and in September 1992 he founded Yeshivat Har Bracha. He is best known as the author of the multi-volume Peninei Halakha series and also writes the Revivim column.

name: ר׳ עמרם גאון
bio: ר׳ עמרם גאון, also known as ר׳ עמרם בר ר׳ ששנא, was a major ninth-century Babylonian gaon, halakhic authority and liturgical figure associated with Sura and Mata Mehasia. His exact birth date is not securely known; modern authority data sometimes places it around 810. He studied under ר׳ נטרונאי בן הילאי.
